steps.notes_before: The method has two prompt-steering vector construction options: RESGA uses a dense representation difference between persona-exhibiting and persona-free examples; SAEGA uses SAE latents selected by contrastive activation differences, then combines encoder directions of the top-K latents. The prompt objective is the negative normalized projection of the prompt representation onto the steering vector, with an added fluency penalty based on token cross-entropy. Optimization uses EPO: a population of prompts, one per fluency weight λ, is mutated via gradient-guided token substitutions, evaluated, and periodically restarted to cover the fluency-steering Pareto frontier. The section also says the overall framework is a three-stage pipeline, with later initialization/selection of prompts from the Pareto frontier (Section 3.3), though the figure caption summarizes it as two stages.

The paper adds two EPO initialization strategies: random initialization seeds prompts with uniformly sampled vocabulary tokens and often yields syntactically fragmented or semantically incoherent prompts, while seed initialization starts from a short natural-language phrase loosely related to the target persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy). Seed initialization tends to place prompts in higher-fluency regions of the Pareto frontier without much loss in steering effectiveness, so it is preferred when interpretability is desired. The evaluation protocol scores candidate prompts on held-out validation data by appending them to task inputs and measuring the change in the target behavioral metric. Fluency is explicitly treated as an intrinsic model-based constraint, measured by the prompt’s self cross-entropy under the language model, not as human readability or grammatical correctness. The paper emphasizes reporting performance along the full fluency-steering Pareto frontier, with particular attention to intermediate regions that balance steering and moderate perplexity increases over random-token baselines. It also measures prompt stability by checking whether a prompt consistently reduces the target persona across diverse validation examples. The overall emphasis remains causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 describes a three-stage framework: (1) build a persona steering vector, (2) optimize prompts with fluent gradient ascent, and (3) initialize/select prompts on a Pareto frontier. RESGA uses a dense residual/representation difference vector \(v_{repr}\) computed as the mean activation difference between persona-exhibiting and persona-free sets. SAEGA uses SAE latent directions: choose the top-K latents by absolute contrastive activation difference and combine their encoder directions \(w_i\) weighted by activation differences. Latent activation is \(a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)\). The steering objective for a prompt is the negative normalized inner product \(f(t)=-\langle e(t),v\rangle/\|e(t)\|\). Fluency is added as a cross-entropy penalty weighted by \(\lambda\), yielding \(\mathcal L_\lambda\). EPO maintains M candidate prompts, computes gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, proposes top-k token substitutions, evaluates candidates for each \(\lambda_i\), and uses periodic restarts. The section claims this explores the fluency–effectiveness Pareto frontier.

This subsection covers initialization, selection, and evaluation. Two EPO initializations are described: random initialization samples vocabulary tokens uniformly and often yields fragmented/incoherent prompts; seed initialization starts from a short natural-language phrase related to the persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy) and is claimed to place optimization closer to the language manifold. Seed-initialized prompts are said to occupy higher-fluency Pareto-frontier regions without much loss in steering effectiveness.

Candidate prompts are evaluated by appending them to held-out validation inputs and measuring the change in the target behavioral metric. The section emphasizes that strong prompts can be fragmented, multilingual, or semantically incoherent.

Fluency is defined as a model-based intrinsic constraint measured by the prompt’s self cross-entropy; lower cross-entropy means closer to the training distribution and higher cross-entropy means more off-manifold. The paper explicitly distinguishes fluency from human readability/grammar. final_notes: Section 6 limitations: RESGA and SAEGA require labeled positive/negative persona examples. Their SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific, so retraining is needed for each target model. There is a fluency-effectiveness tradeoff: the most effective prompts tend to lack semantic coherence, and stronger linguistic priors/constraints may help generate prompts that are both effective and human-like. The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for steering LLM personas. It proposes two methods: RESGA (Residual Gradient Ascent), which uses dense residual representations, and SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent), which uses sparse autoencoder features. Both derive persona directions from contrasting examples and optimize prompts under a fluency constraint. The paper evaluates sycophancy (agreement with incorrect user opinion), hallucination via TruthfulQA error, and myopic reward (short-term reward seeking over long-term outcomes). It claims improvements across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3. The abstract is said to report sycophancy improvement numbers of 49.90% and 79.24%. Mechanistic analyses claim SAEGA suppresses relevant features, concentrates behavior near neutrality, and preserves natural activation sparsity. Limitations mentioned: labeled data dependence, model-specific steering directions, and prompt coherence.

The paper introduces terminology for persona steering in LLMs, especially sycophancy, hallucination (TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward. It distinguishes dense residual steering (RESGA) from sparse-autoencoder steering (SAEGA), both found via contrastive examples and optimized with a fluency constraint. It also covers related concepts such as prompt optimization, mechanistic interpretability, sparse features, and gradient-guided discrete search. The experimental models are Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Gemma 3 4B Instruct. The paper uses baselines like zero-shot, standard prompt, dense steering vector, random direction, and task-loss optimization. It defines evaluation via conditional log-probability comparisons and behavioral metrics such as error rate, with neutralization for sycophancy at 50% error. It also describes prompt discovery components like EPO, mutation, restarts, population, and Pareto frontier, plus future directions and risks such as jailbreak discovery and access controls.

The paper’s title is “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” The abstract proposes two representation-guided prompt-search methods: RESGA (dense residual representations) and SAEGA (sparse autoencoder features). Both use gradient ascent on randomly initialized prompts to align prompt representations with a persona direction, with a fluency constraint called fluent gradient ascent. The paper reports experiments across three model families—Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3—on three personas: sycophancy, hallucination (TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward. The abstract states that automatic prompt discovery improves sycophancy, giving 49.90% compared with 79.24%. The release includes RESGA and SAEGA scripts on GitHub.

Section 1 motivates the paper by contrasting prompt-based steering, activation steering, and the proposed methods. RESGA and SAEGA are introduced as fluent-gradient-ascent prompt-search methods guided by internal representations: RESGA uses dense residual-stream differences, while SAEGA uses sparse autoencoder latents/features. The paper frames the goal as discovering prompts that selectively activate persona-related internal features and steer away from undesirable personas.

Key claims in this section: (1) automatic prompt discovery is more interpretable than black-box prompt optimization; (2) gradient ascent over discrete prompts is challenging because token-space optimization can go off-manifold; and (3) the proposed methods are intended to improve sycophancy and myopic reward while avoiding distributional shifts from dense activation steering.

The section also states that discovered prompts substantially outperform manual prompting and dense steering. The notes already record Table 1 evidence cited here: Standard Prompt avg 55.45, Dense Steering Vector avg 56.10, RESGA avg 45.83, SAEGA avg 46.44; RESGA sycophancy 49.86/50.63/62.65 and myopic reward 38.50/38.50/34.50 across Llama/Qwen/Gemma; SAEGA sycophancy 49.84/49.95/70.70 and myopic reward 31.50/40.50/38.50.

In Section 3, the paper defines a three-stage framework: construct a persona steering vector (from dense representations or SAE latents), optimize fluent prompts with gradient ascent/EPO, and initialize/select prompts from the Pareto frontier. A contradiction appears between Figure 2’s stated objective \(L_{\lambda}=f+H\) and Eq. (4), which defines \(L_{\lambda}=f-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum H\).

Section 3’s prompt-optimization/selection discussion now covers EPO initialization and evaluation. Two initialization strategies are used: random token sampling, which tends to yield fragmented or incoherent prompts, and seed initialization from a short natural-language phrase related to the persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy). Seed starts are said to place optimization nearer the language manifold and to produce higher-fluency prompts without much loss in steering effectiveness.

Candidate prompts are evaluated on held-out validation inputs by appending the prompt and measuring change in the target behavioral metric. Fluency is defined as an intrinsic model-based constraint measured by self cross-entropy; lower cross-entropy means closer to the training distribution, higher cross-entropy means more off-manifold. The paper says it does not use a hard fluency threshold but reports the full Pareto frontier of steering vs. fluency, with downstream analyses focusing on intermediate prompts that balance steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines.

They also evaluate prompt stability, i.e., how consistently a prompt reduces the persona across diverse validation examples, to avoid degenerate prompts that only work on narrow inputs. The section emphasizes causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

Claims/evidence noted here: seed initialization yields effective prompts closer to natural language; strong prompts can be fragmented or incoherent (Table 2); and Table 3 seed→optimized rows are cited as evidence for the seed-initialization claim.

Section 4 evaluates persona mitigation with two methods, RESGA and SAEGA, across three tasks: sycophancy, hallucination (TruthfulQA multiple-choice), and myopic reward. Lower metrics are better throughout. Models are Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Gemma 3 4B Instruct; SAEGA uses pretrained SAEs from SAELens. Baselines are Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, and ProTeGi.

Implementation details: steering targets Layer 25 for Llama/Qwen and Layer 20 for Gemma, justified as middle-to-late layers with higher semantic abstraction; early layers are said to be ineffective and final layers often fail due to accumulated logit bias. All reported experiments use population size M=100, prompt length n=8, and T=1000 iterations. Context-aware optimization appends candidate prompts to a dynamic batch of task-specific questions so the prompt generalizes across contexts. SAEGA selects top-K latents correlated with the concept using activation differences between positive and negative examples; K=20 is reported as consistently strong, against SAE sparsity L0≈50. All results use held-out validation splits.

Evaluation uses conditional log-probability comparison between candidate answers; the metric is the fraction of examples where the model prefers the undesirable option. In the results intro, 50% sycophancy error is defined as perfect neutralization (not behavioral reversal).

steps.notes_before: The method has three stages: persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained prompt discovery, and validation-based selection/frontier analysis. For persona vectors, the paper contrasts dense residual-stream differences with sparse SAE-based directions. The SAE version uses contrastive relevance between persona-positive and persona-negative datasets, selecting the largest absolute differences and forming a direction from SAE encoder weights. For discovery, it uses an evolutionary gradient-based search over token sequences to optimize a persona-reduction objective plus a fluency term. The objective is defined as the negative projection of a prompt representation onto the target persona direction, normalized by representation norm, and fluency is enforced by subtracting next-token cross-entropy weighted by λ. The paper says low cross-entropy means closer to the model’s training distribution and that no hard fluency threshold is imposed; prompts are evaluated across the frontier. Initialization matters: random token starts often yield fragmented prompts, while short natural-language seeds can keep search in more interpretable regions without much loss in steering.

Section 4 evaluates whether discovered prompts neutralize undesirable personas, compares residual vs SAE steering, and examines interpretability/stability. Tasks: B2R (sycophancy), U9K (TruthfulQA hallucination/error), and D6V (myopic reward), with lower fractions better. Models are C7N (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct), W4X (Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct), and F9S (Gemma 3 4B Instruct); V7P refers to the SAE-based method using pretrained SAELens autoencoders. Baselines are zero-shot, a standard prompt (“Answer honestly”), dense steering vectors, H2F, and Z6Q. Interventions use middle-to-late layers (25/25/20 for C7N/W4X/F9S), with N8C population 100, prompt length 8, and 1000 iterations. Evaluation compares ​log P(a|q,p)​ for candidate answers and uses held-out validation splits.

Results: QX2 and V7P both bring B2R close to neutralization (~50%) across models. They also improve U9K and D6V over baselines; QX2 is especially strong on U9K, while V7P gives the best C7N D6V reduction. Table 1 reports averages of 45.83 for QX2 and 46.44 for V7P.

This part gives qualitative analyses of steering mechanisms. It contrasts P8D, QX2, and V7P: baseline B2R projections show agreement bias; P8D and QX2 shift the mean toward neutrality but keep substantial variance, while V7P sharply concentrates near neutrality. In SAE space, P8D causes a feature-count explosion, QX2 partially mitigates but still increases sparsity, and V7P stays near baseline sparsity. Feature-level and PCA analyses likewise present V7P as more selective, stable, and on-manifold than P8D/QX2.

Table 2 lists randomly initialized discovered prompts for B2R, U9K, and D6V under QX2 and V7P. Table 3 shows seed-initialized N8C optimization: in every example, the optimized prompt score is lower than the seed score (e.g., 69.16%→56.25%, 72.30%→54.22%). Table 4 reports WikiText2/T9B perplexity before vs after prepending discovered prompts: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19.

Section 4.4 says seed initialization preserves more natural-language structure and interpretability, while discovered prompts still steer effectively. It also claims general language-model perplexity changes are negligible overall. Mechanistically, the paper describes Y2H/token priming for some QX2 prompts and G6T/semantic steering for V7P.

This part adds qualitative interpretations of two prompts: B2R/polite disagreement, where V7P suppresses affirmative tokens like “Yes,” “True,” and “Agree” and upweights “However” and “But”; and D6V/temporal priming, where QX2 and V7P upweight “Future,” “Long,” and “Wait.” Section 4.5 then reports ablations: K3Y (random direction), E8U (random mutation), and M5A (task-loss objective). final_notes: Conclusion: RESGA and SAEGA are presented as automatic persona-steering prompt discovery methods that build steering vectors from labeled examples and optimize prompts via evolutionary gradient ascent. The paper claims they improve sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic reward, and outperform standard/manual prompting and dense steering. Mechanistic analysis says SAEGA neutralizes behavior while preserving natural activation manifolds and controlling interpretable features. Evidence cited: Table 1 average scores (RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44 vs Standard Prompt 55.45 and Dense Steering 56.10) and Figures 3–6 (near-zero neutrality, ~50 baseline active features vs >150 for dense steering, 50–60 for SAEGA, selective suppression, stable geometry). Limitations: the methods require labeled examples with and without the target persona, are model-specific and need retraining for each target model, and the most effective prompts often lack semantic coherence. The authors suggest stronger linguistic priors could improve fluency while maintaining effectiveness. Future directions include semi-supervised methods to reduce labels, cross-model transferability, and multi-persona steering. Broader impact: the work is framed as improving LLM safety by suppressing undesired personas, but it could also be misused to find jailbreaks or elicit harmful outputs, so access controls are recommended. The formal equation defines \(\mathcal L_\lambda(t)=f(t)-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum H(\cdot)\), where \(f(t)\) is the negative normalized projection onto the steering vector. EPO maintains a population of \(M\) prompts, mutates them using top-gradient token substitutions, and uses restarts to avoid premature convergence. The paper claims this procedure improves Llama myopic-reward error by 23.50 points over random mutation while exploring fluency–effectiveness tradeoffs.

The paper’s selection stage for persona-steering prompts uses two initialization strategies: random token sampling and seed initialization from a short natural-language phrase related to the persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy). Seed starts are described as higher-fluency and more interpretable, while random starts often produce fragmented/incoherent prompts. The paper says EPO candidates span a fluency–steering Pareto frontier, and validation evaluates how a prompt changes the target behavioral metric when appended to held-out inputs. Fluency is not readability; it is model-based self cross-entropy, where lower cross-entropy means closer to the model’s training distribution. They prefer reporting the whole Pareto frontier rather than a hard fluency cutoff, and emphasize intermediate prompts with moderate perplexity increases over random-token baselines. They also evaluate prompt stability across diverse validation examples to avoid degenerate solutions.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 describes a three-stage framework: (1) build a persona steering vector, (2) optimize prompts with fluent gradient ascent, and (3) initialize/select prompts on a Pareto frontier. RESGA uses a dense residual/representation difference vector \(v_{repr}\) computed as the mean activation difference between persona-exhibiting and persona-free sets. SAEGA uses SAE latent directions: choose the top-K latents by absolute contrastive activation difference and combine their encoder directions \(w_i\) weighted by activation differences. Latent activation is \(a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)\). The steering objective for a prompt is the negative normalized inner product \(f(t)=-\langle e(t),v\rangle/\|e(t)\|\). Fluency is added as a cross-entropy penalty weighted by \(\lambda\), yielding \(\mathcal L_\lambda\). EPO maintains M candidate prompts, computes gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, proposes top-k token substitutions, evaluates candidates for each \(\lambda_i\), and uses periodic restarts. The section claims this explores the fluency–effectiveness Pareto frontier.

This subsection covers initialization, selection, and evaluation. Two EPO initializations are described: random initialization samples vocabulary tokens uniformly and often yields fragmented/incoherent prompts; seed initialization starts from a short natural-language phrase related to the persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy) and is claimed to place optimization closer to the language manifold. Seed-initialized prompts are said to occupy higher-fluency Pareto-frontier regions without much loss in steering effectiveness.

Candidate prompts are evaluated by appending them to held-out validation inputs and measuring the change in the target behavioral metric. The section emphasizes that strong prompts can be fragmented, multilingual, or semantically incoherent.

Fluency is defined as a model-based intrinsic constraint measured by the prompt’s self cross-entropy; lower cross-entropy means closer to the training distribution and higher cross-entropy means more off-manifold. The paper explicitly distinguishes fluency from human readability/grammar. Rather than using a hard fluency threshold, results are reported across the full Pareto frontier, with downstream analyses focusing on intermediate prompts that balance steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines.

They also evaluate prompt stability: consistency of persona reduction across diverse validation examples, to avoid prompts that work only on narrow subsets. The stated goal is to prioritize causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 describes a three-stage framework: (1) build a persona steering vector, (2) optimize prompts with fluent gradient ascent, and (3) initialize/select prompts on a Pareto frontier. RESGA uses a dense residual/representation difference vector \(v_{repr}\) computed as the mean activation difference between persona-exhibiting and persona-free sets. SAEGA uses SAE latent directions: choose the top-K latents by absolute contrastive activation difference and combine their encoder directions \(w_i\) weighted by activation differences. Latent activation is \(a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i)\). The steering objective for a prompt is the negative normalized inner product \(f(t)=-\langle e(t),v\rangle/\|e(t)\|\). Fluency is added as a cross-entropy penalty weighted by \(\lambda\), yielding \(\mathcal L_\lambda\). EPO maintains M candidate prompts, computes gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, proposes top-k token substitutions, evaluates candidates for each \(\lambda_i\), and uses periodic restarts. The section claims this explores the fluency–effectiveness Pareto frontier.

This subsection covers initialization, selection, and evaluation. Two EPO initializations are described: random initialization samples vocabulary tokens uniformly and often yields fragmented/incoherent prompts; seed initialization starts from a short natural-language phrase related to the persona (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy) and is claimed to place optimization closer to the language manifold. Seed-initialized prompts are said to occupy higher-fluency Pareto-frontier regions without much loss in steering effectiveness.

Candidate prompts are evaluated by appending them to held-out validation inputs and measuring the change in the target behavioral metric. The section emphasizes that strong prompts can be fragmented, multilingual, or semantically incoherent.

Fluency is defined as a model-based intrinsic constraint measured by the prompt’s self cross-entropy; lower cross-entropy means closer to the training distribution and higher cross-entropy means more off-manifold. The paper explicitly distinguishes fluency from human readability/grammar. Rather than using a hard fluency threshold, results are reported across the full Pareto frontier, with downstream analyses focusing on intermediate prompts that balance steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines.

They also evaluate prompt stability: consistency of persona reduction across diverse validation examples, to avoid prompts that work only on narrow subsets. The stated goal is to prioritize causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

The paper proposes a framework that bridges mechanistic interpretability and prompt engineering by performing gradient ascent on randomly initialized prompts toward identified persona directions. It emphasizes targeted, interpretable prompt discovery and includes a fluency-control component for the resulting prompts. The approach is evaluated on two groups of tasks/benchmarks and claims strong mitigation gains, including B2R mitigation. The introduction contrasts manual prompting, dense activation steering, and its proposed residual-stream (QX2/RESGA) and SAE-based (V7P/SAEGA) optimization methods, arguing that prompt-based steering avoids distributional shifts seen with dense steering. It also frames the work as a new paradigm for controllable, interpretable behavior modification and mentions a public code repository.

The paper’s related-work section situates the method among three areas: persona steering, sparse autoencoders, and prompt engineering. Persona-steering work includes RLHF and constitutional AI; RepE and CAA are cited as activation-steering approaches, with applications to B2R mitigation, toxicity, and bias, plus SAE-based persona features for control. The SAE section emphasizes interpretable sparse features and architectural variants such as JumpReLU, Top-K, Batch Top-K, and Matryoshka SAEs. The prompt-engineering section reviews in-context prompting, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, Program-Aided Language models/Program of Thoughts, evolutionary prompt optimization with fluency control, socially grounded agents, optimal-control views of prompting, ProTeGi, and GCG.

Section 3 presents a three-stage method: (1) build persona-steering vectors, either by direct representation difference or from SAE latents; (2) discover prompts with a fluency-constrained evolutionary/gradient method called J4Z / N8C; and (3) initialize and select prompts using validation performance. The SAE-based vector uses contrastive relevance of latent activations between persona-positive and persona-negative sets, selecting the top-K absolute differences and combining them with encoder weights. The direct alternative is the difference of mean hidden representations. The steering objective is the negative normalized projection of a prompt’s last-token representation onto the persona vector, so maximizing it pushes representations away from the target persona. Fluency is enforced with a cross-entropy penalty from the language model; lower self-cross-entropy means more natural prompts. The algorithm maintains a population of prompts across different lambda values, mutates candidates using token gradients, and uses restarts to avoid premature convergence. For better interpretability, the method prefers short natural-language seed prompts (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for B2R) over random-token initialization. Evaluation uses held-out validation inputs and focuses on prompts along the fluency–steering frontier, emphasizing both steering effectiveness and stability across diverse examples.

steps.notes_before: The method has three stages: (1) construct a persona steering vector from either dense representation differences (RESGA) or SAE latents (SAEGA), (2) use fluent gradient ascent to find prompts that steer away from the persona while staying readable, and (3) initialize/select prompts on a fluency–steering Pareto frontier using validation performance. For RESGA, the steering vector is the difference between mean activations of persona-exhibiting and persona-free examples. For SAEGA, the method compares latent activations on the two sets, selects the top-K latents by absolute mean difference, and combines their encoder directions weighted by those differences. Fluent gradient ascent uses an objective combining a persona-reduction score with a fluency penalty, and EPO maintains a population of prompts, applies gradient-guided token substitutions, and uses periodic restarts to explore tradeoffs.

EPO uses two initialization strategies: random starts (uniform token sampling, often fragmented or incoherent) and seed starts (short natural-language phrases related to the persona, e.g. “Please answer honestly” for sycophancy). Seeded prompts are described as staying closer to the language manifold and occupying higher-fluency Pareto-frontier regions without significantly reducing steering effectiveness, making them preferable for interpretability. Candidate prompts are appended to held-out validation inputs and evaluated by their change in the target behavioral metric. Fluency is model-based and measured by self cross-entropy / perplexity; lower cross-entropy means closer to the model’s training distribution. The paper reports results across the full Pareto frontier rather than using a hard fluency threshold, and emphasizes intermediate prompts with measurable steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. Prompt stability is also evaluated across diverse validation examples to avoid degenerate prompts that only work on a narrow subset.

final_notes: Part 4.3: Baselines C6W=random and U9F=majority; H3D=icl uses same-topic examples or random subset under context limits. ZP4 is generally strongest: it beats naive and V7K on all datasets except T9A on M8C, and is comparable to or better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q is easiest, M8C hardest; binary J4Q likely helps, and R2V > M8C may reflect more training samples. Reasoning support is not consistently helpful: T9A > K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E is best overall, and QX2 trails ZP4. Part 4.4: Agents usually give coherent pro/con arguments matching final answers; failures include illogical or hallucinated content and inconsistency across topics. Part 4.5: Groupwise F1 shows J4Q advantage for P7N over A4U/X8J. R2V/M8C show similar but weaker patterns; on R2V P7N and A4U are about equal, and M8C is lower overall. V7K averages are highest for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Part 4.6: Neutral recall is worst for every M8C individual. X8J has the highest Neutral rate and greatest difficulty; A4U also tends toward Neutral. Removing Neutral instances improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U gaps, and improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but P7N–X8J differences remain. Neutral rate correlates negatively with performance. Part 4.7: Agents do not perfectly represent candidates. No overall left shift; positions move center-right horizontally and centerward vertically, with an overall conservative negative-y trend. X8J shifts more left-wing, while P7N/A4U shift more right-wing/conservative. Part 4.8: Progressive bias mainly hurts underrepresented views rather than helping overrepresented ones. Progressive prompts harm X8J; conservative prompts harm P7N with no consistent X8J gain. Bias-induced positional shifts are strongest for underrepresented groups, and default vs conservative-biased data look very similar. Part 4.9: Inversion on J4Q rotates positions about 180° and flips right-wing to left-wing positions. It helps X8J but hurts P7N/A4U; P7N worsens on average while X8J improves but still stays below original P7N F1, so the disparity remains. Conclusion: ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, and related settings.

Part 1 introduces the paper, titled “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” The abstract claims that structured reasoning trained through reinforcement learning makes LLMs produce profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics, remains competitive with strong baselines, and still leaves bias that needs additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. It also says released methods and datasets establish a research baseline.

Part 2 introduces the motivation and setup for opinion alignment via reasoning. It claims survey-trained agents can generate short rationales plus choices and, through reinforcement learning on matching respondents’ answers, learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. The paper frames recent RL successes (e.g., o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) as motivation.

It argues that accurate political digital twins require simulation of individual political behavior, but current LLM political discourse and demographic prompts do not reliably represent human viewpoint diversity or real distributions. Preference-consistency methods use known individual opinions instead of demographic proxies; interview transcripts can perform well but are costly and hard to scale.

Large surveys and Voting Advice Applications are presented as scalable sources of political positions, useful for bias evaluation and group simulation, but underused for individual-agent training.

The stated contributions are: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; a released benchmark with authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; and answer-inversion analysis showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Figure 1 sketches a pipeline where synthetic-statement fine-tuning establishes a reasoning template before QX2 improves reasoning with formatting/correctness rewards.

Part 3 reviews related work. It distinguishes political-persona prompting into demographic, character, and individualized personas, arguing individualized personas are most relevant for individual modeling but are rare. Demographic prompting includes simple party labels, richer demographic descriptions, belief-network demonstrations, and combinations with preference optimization (ORPO). Limitations of demographic personas include poor representativeness, weak steerability, and inconsistency across topics, with prompt sensitivity and missing within-group variance. Beyond demographics, interview-based public-opinion modeling can outperform demographic baselines but is limited by transcript availability; another line uses respondents’ Q&A pairs for bias identification rather than full opinion modeling.

The section includes an illustrative table showing a model shifting from disagreement to agreement on inequality while retaining equal-opportunity reasoning under a different framing. It then summarizes reasoning methods: CoT and “Let’s think step by step” improve accuracy, and RL methods like GRPO/QX2 sample multiple outputs and use group-relative reward normalization. Finally, it situates the paper relative to persona-based voting simulations: prior work combines demographic, ideological, and temporal factors with CoT-style prompting calibrated on M8C, but does not use RL and targets voting rather than broad preference profiles.

Part 4 introduces the method. Given a policy question q, persona p (respondent or party), and stance set {No, Neutral, Yes}, the task is individual alignment: learn p’s stance on q. The system prompt includes only a country label and no explicit persona representation. Training data are tuples (p, q, y*), with no reasoning annotations. The model must output a reasoning trace and an answer in the exact schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Reward combines format correctness (E6Z), length closeness to a target length (F2B = -|L-L*|), and answer correctness (G9L = indicator of matching the observed stance), with correctness weighted highest (α3=1, α1=0.25, α2=0.01). An optional supervised warm start uses SFT on chain-of-thought demonstrations in the rewarded schema. Table 2 lists datasets: J4Q (CH) candidates, binary labels; R2V (DE) parties, ternary labels; M8C 2020 (US) respondents, ternary labels.

Part 4.1 reports evaluation on J4Q (Swiss smartvote), R2V (German Wahl-O-Mat), and M8C (2020 ANES), and Table 3 gives macro-F1 at T=1.0 over 8 stochastic runs for untrained baselines and several methods/backbones. It uses public political surveys as preference profiles, especially ANES (U.S.) and VAAs such as smartvote, and compares this approach to demographic-prompting methods and interview-based persona modeling. The introduction frames the goal as preference consistency rather than demographic proxying. Contributions: (1) reinforcement learning for reasoning-based opinion alignment, (2) benchmarking on German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates, and (3) analysis of ideological effects via answer inversion. The paper claims reasoning improves alignment, but there are exceptions (explicitly noted for Llama 3.1 8B on ANES).

The paper cites three limitations of demographic approaches: representativeness, steerability, and consistency. steps.notes_before: Section 3 introduces the method for survey stance learning. It defines stance labels \(Y\) (e.g., Yes/Neutral/No) and says the goal is to learn a persona’s stance on a question. GRPO is used with a fixed output schema: `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. Training data are tuples \((p_j,q_i,y^*_{ij})\) containing personas, questions, and observed stances, with no reasoning traces. Reward has three parts: format reward for correct tags (4 max), length reward \(-|L-L^*|\) with max 0 at the target length, and correctness reward \(\mathds{1}[y_i=y_i^*]\), combined with weights 0.25, 0.01, and 1. The system prompt uses only a country label; there is no explicit persona representation. Optional SFT before GRPO provides chain-of-thought demonstrations in the same format to warm-start formatting and reasoning. Table 2 summarizes datasets: smartvote (CH) candidate units (18, binary labels, 48 train/12 test topic-stratified), WoM (DE) party units (6, 30 test, train counts in Table 5), and ANES 2020 (US) respondent units (21, 67 train/12 test random).

Section 4 introduces experiments across three datasets: WoM (German party positions), ANES 2020 (U.S. respondents), and smartvote (Swiss candidates). Table 3 reports mean macro-F1 over 8 stochastic runs at T=1.0, computed per unit then averaged; F1 is the main metric used in figures.

Dataset details: WoM uses six major German parties (CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), maps agree/neutral/disagree to {Yes, Neutral, No}, and evaluates out-of-domain on EU&I 2024 (30 items). ANES uses 79 policy items, two recoding schemes to {Yes, Neutral, No} (conservative default), 67 train / 12 test questions, and 21 respondents sampled from the 7-point ideology question. smartvote uses the English 2023 Swiss national election questionnaire with 75 items, 60 policy questions across 12 topics, collapsed to binary {Yes, No}, and 18 candidates sampled from six parties.

Table 3 shows best overall performance for SFT+GRPO across all datasets/backbones, with smartvote scores highest overall and WoM generally outperforming ANES. For Llama 3.1 8B, SFT+GRPO reaches 66.88 on smartvote, 52.53 on WoM, and 40.66 on ANES; Qwen3 8B reaches 65.11, 49.38, and 38.44; Magistral 24B reaches 70.73, 53.21, and 45.43. The paper attributes smartvote’s stronger scores to binary labels and no Neutral class, and WoM’s advantage over ANES to more training samples.

Section 5 discusses limitations and future work. Limitations: human opinion noise means F1 near 1.0 is unlikely; separate per-profile training is computationally expensive; suitable surveys are scarce, often too small or not aligned across countries. Future work: use compact persona representations in a single model to reduce cost and improve data use; add confidence/reliability estimates via extended reasoning or a dedicated value head; better uncertainty handling and purpose-built questionnaires may help with Neutral. The method frames individual-level alignment as learning survey stances from persona-question-answer triples, using GRPO to reward three components: output format, reasoning length near a target, and correct final answers. The required output schema is <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>, and the total reward is a weighted sum with weights α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. The paper says there is no explicit persona representation; the system prompt includes only a country label, and alignment comes from answering questions correctly. It also optionally uses supervised fine-tuning before GRPO with chain-of-thought demonstrations in the same format to improve format learning and initialization. It argues that although the two can look similar in output space, they produce different internal activations, and that ICL activations may contain useful information for generalizable adaptation. The proposed method has three steps: collect ICL activations, enforce alignment with ICL’s functional behavior, then perform SFT on the primed model. The paper defines a decoder-only transformer LM with self-attention weights W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O (grouped as W_QKVO). For a token sequence T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R, causal self-attention uses past tokens t_:i and outputs Z with the same shape as T. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) uses input-output pairs (X_i, Y_i), updates weights Θ→Θ′, and minimizes cross-entropy over generated response tokens. In-context learning (ICL) uses a prompt I made of concatenated demo pairs [X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] plus a test input Xt, with no weight updates, to produce a task-appropriate response. The paper defines activations as hidden self-attention outputs; for a model with L layers and R tokens, activation tensor A has size L×R×d. It studies activations for sequences [I∘X] under ICL and X without ICL, across different model weights, and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, yielding an L×R matrix.

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not practically equivalent. It reports an experiment comparing ICL activations A_ICL (from prompts T=[I∘X]) with SFT activations A_SFT (from T=X) across 100 test samples, multiple datasets, and several Qwen3/Llama-3.2 model sizes. The paper says token-level activation similarity (asim) between ICL and SFT is low overall, with better alignment in early and final layers and poorer alignment in the middle layers. It also claims ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar, slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be treated as a drop-in replacement for ICL. The section motivates a research question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, and says the proposed IA2→SFT pipeline will do so.

Section 4 proposes a two-step training pipeline to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. Step 1, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), aims to make the SFT model’s attention behavior match ICL by learning modified weights \tilde{W}_{QKVO} so that SA([I∘X];W_{QKVO}) ≈ SA(X;\tilde{W}_{QKVO}) for newly generated tokens. The paper says prior work has a closed-form solution in linearized attention, but here they optimize a practical non-linear version. IA2 is implemented by generating ICL responses \hat{Y}_i for training inputs X_i, collecting ICL activations A_ICL^i over output positions, then running the same queries with only X_i concatenated with \hat{Y}_i to obtain activations A^i, and minimizing MSE between A^i and A_ICL^i. Step 2 continues standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y after IA2, using the updated model parameters \Theta'. The pipeline is summarized as: (1) align activations to ICL until convergence, then (2) switch to SFT loss on target responses until convergence.

The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

They collected ICL activations A_ICL from T=[I∘X] on 100 test samples from datasets including SST2 and AGNews, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models (1B/16 layers, 3B/28 layers, 4B/36 layers). They trained SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence and collected A_SFT with T=X. Using asim at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets, they report low similarity between ICL and SFT; similarity is higher in early and late layers and lower in middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated than SFT at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes that SFT should not replace ICL directly and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT in the next section.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 introduces IA2, a two-step method to make SFT models behave more like ICL. IA2 first aligns internal activations: for each training sample Xi, the model generates an ICL response Yi-hat using demonstrations T_i=[I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL, then runs the model on [X_i∘Y_i-hat] without demonstrations to get A^i and trains to match A^i to A_ICL. After IA2, the model is further trained with standard SFT cross-entropy on ground-truth targets Y_i. Section 5 describes the experimental setup. It compares IA2 and baselines on single-token and multi-token tasks, emphasizing both ID and OOD evaluation. Section 6 discusses alternatives and baselines. Table 3 reports that, relative to ground-truth training, all response-based methods drop, but IA2+SFT still outperforms SFT-only on GSM8K, GSM8Ks*, HMathA, and SciQ; IA2-only is best on GSM8K, while IA2+SFT is best on the other tasks. The paper next compares training on ICL-generated responses versus ground-truth labels. The paper’s related-work section positions IA2 among ICL-vs-SFT comparisons, context distillation, and activation steering. Paper proposes IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) to improve supervised fine-tuning by aligning SFT model activations with those produced by in-context learning. The introduction argues that although ICL and SFT can look similar in token outputs, they differ internally: models produce disparate activation patterns under ICL vs. SFT, and these activations are treated as a footprint of functional behavior. IA2 is presented as a self-distillation method with three steps: collect ICL activations, enforce alignment with ICL’s functional behavior, then perform SFT on the primed model. The authors claim this priming step before SFT improves downstream performance on text classification and generation tasks and provides a training signal absent in SFT-only training. They report training over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks.

The paper defines a standard decoder-only transformer LM with self-attention and linear layers, and gives notation for attention weights W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O. It describes SFT on a task dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)} by fine-tuning parameters to produce responses for new inputs, with an SFT loss written as token-level cross-entropy over generated tokens. It defines ICL as prompting the model with concatenated demonstrations I=[X_1∘Y_1∘…∘X_n∘Y_n] plus a query X_t, producing an output without weight updates. Activations are the hidden self-attention outputs across layers/tokens, represented as an L×R×d tensor, and the paper defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, yielding an L×R matrix. The broader paper goal remains IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment): align SFT model activations with those from ICL to improve downstream performance.

The paper argues that ICL and SFT are not functionally the same despite recent claims of equivalence via internal gradient descent. In experiments, it compares ICL activations A_ICL (from T=[I∘X]) against SFT activations A_SFT (from T=X) on 100 test samples from multiple datasets and several Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 model sizes. Using activation similarity (asim), it finds that ICL and SFT activations are not well aligned overall, with better alignment near the initial and final layers and worse alignment in the middle. The paper also claims ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be treated as a drop-in replacement for ICL. This motivates the research question of whether ICL activations can be used to improve SFT, leading to the proposed IA2 → SFT pipeline.

Section 4 introduces R8D = IA2, a priming method meant to align layerwise processing rather than output similarity. It seeks adapted Q/K/V/O weights so that SA([I∘X]; W_QKVO) ≈ SA(X; \tilde W_QKVO) for the newly generated token at index -1. The text says Chen et al. (2024a) provide a closed-form linearized-attention solution, but this paper aims for a practical nonlinear-transformer version. For each training sample X_i, it constructs I from the remaining dataset, generates \hat Y_i from [I∘X_i], and collects V2K output-position activations A^i_V2K for G response tokens. It then supplies [X_i∘\hat Y_i] to obtain unaligned output-position activations A^i and minimizes the MSE ||A^i - A^i_V2K|| until convergence.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. All methods/dataset combinations are trained up to 50 epochs at three learning rates, with the best learning rate selected; over 13,000 models were trained. Rank-8 LoRAs target SA matrices W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token runs are more expensive, so N is capped at 16 for Llama and 8 for Qwen. Activation collection uses G=200 by default, yielding \hat A_i \in R^{L\times 200\times d}; target-token training instead uses the ground-truth response length. Single-token evaluation uses first-token probabilities for accuracy (U6R) and calibration (D8P/ECE); base models with demonstrations are evaluated five times and averaged, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations. Multi-token evaluation only considers correctly answered, correctly formatted outputs and does not measure calibration. Qwen3-4B-Base is used on all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B is used for all single-token tasks except E2T (which needs Llama-3.2-3B because 1B stays near random), and multi-token experiments use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Tasks include sentiment, StrategyQA, AGNews/BBCNews, MCQ with remapped option tokens (E2T from SciQ and G6A from QASC), GSM8K/GSM Symbolic, MATH Algebra, and SciQ. Few-shot training uses N in powers of two with five random sets per N and shared training data across methods. Multi-token outputs use chain-of-thought style parsing; L9S/X4C require the exact numerical answer after '####', V7B uses \boxed{}, and O3D uses support text plus exact text-answer matching. Section 5.1 reports that one method outperforms another in most single-token cases on accuracy and calibration, with another often matching V2K-like calibration without target-response-token training.

The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

Paper introduces IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) to improve supervised fine-tuning by aligning SFT model activations with those produced by in-context learning. Abstract claims: (1) ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, suggesting different functional mechanisms; (2) IA2 is a self-distillation technique that replicates ICL activation patterns in SFT models and incentivizes ICL-like internal reasoning; (3) applying IA2 as a priming step before SFT improves accuracy and calibration; (4) experiments cover 12 popular benchmarks and two model families.

Paper proposes IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) to improve supervised fine-tuning by aligning SFT model activations with those produced by in-context learning. The introduction argues that although ICL and SFT can look similar in token outputs, they differ internally: models produce disparate activation patterns under ICL vs. SFT, and these activations are treated as a footprint of functional behavior. IA2 is presented as a self-distillation method with three steps: collect ICL activations, enforce alignment with ICL’s functional behavior, then perform SFT on the primed model. The authors claim this priming step before SFT improves downstream performance on text classification and generation tasks and provides a training signal absent in SFT-only training. They report training over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks.

The paper defines a standard decoder-only transformer LM with self-attention and linear layers, and gives notation for attention weights W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O. It describes SFT on a task dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)} by fine-tuning parameters to produce responses for new inputs, with an SFT loss written as token-level cross-entropy over generated tokens. It defines ICL as prompting the model with concatenated demonstrations I=[X_1∘Y_1∘…∘X_n∘Y_n] plus a query X_t, producing an output without weight updates. Activations are the hidden self-attention outputs across layers/tokens, represented as an L×R×d tensor, and the paper defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, yielding an L×R matrix. The broader paper goal remains IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment): align SFT model activations with those from ICL to improve downstream performance.

The paper argues that ICL and SFT are not functionally the same despite recent claims of equivalence via internal gradient descent. In experiments, it compares ICL activations A_ICL (from T=[I∘X]) against SFT activations A_SFT (from T=X) on 100 test samples from multiple datasets and several Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 model sizes. Using activation similarity (asim), it finds that ICL and SFT activations are not well aligned overall, with better alignment near the initial and final layers and worse alignment in the middle. The paper also claims ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be treated as a drop-in replacement for ICL. This motivates the research question of whether ICL activations can be used to improve SFT, leading to the proposed IA2 → SFT pipeline.

Training loss sums cross-entropy over G generated tokens. The decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers; SA is defined with W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O and causal prefix tokens t_{:i}. V2K/ICL uses concatenated demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] and produces M_Θ(I∘X_t)=\hat y_t without weight updates; the setting here uses classic input–output pairs. Section 3 argues V2K and Q7M are not practically the same: although V2K responses are more calibrated than Q7M at similar or slightly better output quality, the internal activations do not match across models, especially in middle layers. The section cites internal-gradient-descent interpretations to suggest that if Q7M were functionally equivalent to V2K, output-position activations would be similar, but the observed similarity pattern is instead higher in initial/final layers than in middle layers. Figure 2 compares layerwise similarity (K4X) to V2K activations: H9C shows low similarity, while P4Z aligns much more closely and performs better. The experiment collects A_V2K on 100 test samples from multiple datasets (including B7V and W3F) using T=[I∘X], then trains on the same demonstrations to convergence and collects A_Q7M using T=X. Models span Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 with 1B/16-layer, 3B/28-layer, and 4B/36-layer correspondences; output-position similarity is K4X(A_V2K, A_Q7M).

Section 4 introduces R8D = IA2, a priming method meant to align layerwise processing rather than output similarity. It seeks adapted Q/K/V/O weights so that SA([I∘X]; W_QKVO) ≈ SA(X; \tilde W_QKVO) for the newly generated token at index -1. The text says Chen et al. (2024a) provide a closed-form linearized-attention solution, but this paper aims for a practical nonlinear-transformer version. For each training sample X_i, it constructs I from the remaining dataset, generates \hat Y_i from [I∘X_i], and collects V2K output-position activations A^i_V2K for G response tokens. It then supplies [X_i∘\hat Y_i] to obtain unaligned output-position activations A^i and minimizes the MSE ||A^i - A^i_V2K|| until convergence.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. All methods/dataset combinations are trained up to 50 epochs at three learning rates, with the best learning rate selected; over 13,000 models were trained. Rank-8 LoRAs target SA matrices W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token runs are more expensive, so N is capped at 16 for Llama and 8 for Qwen. Activation collection uses G=200 by default, yielding \hat A_i \in R^{L\times 200\times d}; target-token training instead uses the ground-truth response length. Single-token evaluation uses first-token probabilities for accuracy (U6R) and calibration (D8P/ECE); base models with demonstrations are evaluated five times and averaged, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations. Multi-token evaluation only considers correctly answered, correctly formatted outputs and does not measure calibration. Qwen3-4B-Base is used on all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B is used for all single-token tasks except E2T (which needs Llama-3.2-3B because 1B stays near random), and multi-token experiments use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Tasks include sentiment, StrategyQA, AGNews/BBCNews, MCQ with remapped option tokens (E2T from SciQ and G6A from QASC), GSM8K/GSM Symbolic, MATH Algebra, and SciQ. Few-shot training uses N in powers of two with five random sets per N and shared training data across methods. Multi-token outputs use chain-of-thought style parsing; L9S/X4C require the exact numerical answer after '####', V7B uses \boxed{}, and O3D uses support text plus exact text-answer matching. Section 5.1 reports that one method outperforms another in most single-token cases on accuracy and calibration, with another often matching V2K-like calibration without target-response-token training.
