The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

Paper introduces IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) to improve supervised fine-tuning by aligning SFT model activations with those produced by in-context learning. Abstract claims: (1) ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, suggesting different functional mechanisms; (2) IA2 is a self-distillation technique that replicates ICL activation patterns in SFT models and incentivizes ICL-like internal reasoning; (3) applying IA2 as a priming step before SFT improves accuracy and calibration; (4) experiments cover 12 popular benchmarks and two model families.

Paper proposes IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) to improve supervised fine-tuning by aligning SFT model activations with those produced by in-context learning. The introduction argues that although ICL and SFT can look similar in token outputs, they differ internally: models produce disparate activation patterns under ICL vs. SFT, and these activations are treated as a footprint of functional behavior. IA2 is presented as a self-distillation method with three steps: collect ICL activations, enforce alignment with ICL’s functional behavior, then perform SFT on the primed model. The authors claim this priming step before SFT improves downstream performance on text classification and generation tasks and provides a training signal absent in SFT-only training. They report training over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks.

The paper defines a standard decoder-only transformer LM with self-attention and linear layers, and gives notation for attention weights W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O. It describes SFT on a task dataset D_T={(X_i,Y_i)} by fine-tuning parameters to produce responses for new inputs, with an SFT loss written as token-level cross-entropy over generated tokens. It defines ICL as prompting the model with concatenated demonstrations I=[X_1∘Y_1∘…∘X_n∘Y_n] plus a query X_t, producing an output without weight updates. Activations are the hidden self-attention outputs across layers/tokens, represented as an L×R×d tensor, and the paper defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, yielding an L×R matrix. The broader paper goal remains IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment): align SFT model activations with those from ICL to improve downstream performance.

The paper argues that ICL and SFT are not functionally the same despite recent claims of equivalence via internal gradient descent. In experiments, it compares ICL activations A_ICL (from T=[I∘X]) against SFT activations A_SFT (from T=X) on 100 test samples from multiple datasets and several Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 model sizes. Using activation similarity (asim), it finds that ICL and SFT activations are not well aligned overall, with better alignment near the initial and final layers and worse alignment in the middle. The paper also claims ICL is better calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be treated as a drop-in replacement for ICL. This motivates the research question of whether ICL activations can be used to improve SFT, leading to the proposed IA2 → SFT pipeline.

Main research question: whether information-rich V2K activations can improve Q7M quality. The hypothesis is that these activations encode generalizable contextual patterns that may be absent from few-shot weight adaptation, which can overfit shortcuts or targets. The paper argues matching outputs alone does not guarantee matching internal functioning. Figure 1 frames standard Q7M as output-space agreement between response and target and says it tends to be subpar and miscalibrated under low data; the proposed pipeline instead collects V2K activations, enforces functional alignment, then trains against target responses.

Introduction: the paper asks whether information-rich V2K activations can improve Q7M quality, arguing weight adaptation may overfit shortcuts while matching outputs does not ensure matching internal functioning. Background/notation: task data D_T={ (X_i,Y_i) }_{i=1}^N. Q7M/SFT updates weights Θ→Θ' so M_{Θ'}(X_t)=\bar y_t, the first token of \bar Y_t, with autoregressive continuation generating the full response. Training loss sums cross-entropy over G generated tokens. The decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers; SA is defined with W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O and causal prefix tokens t_{:i}. V2K/ICL uses concatenated demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] and produces M_Θ(I∘X_t)=\hat y_t without weight updates; the setting here uses classic input–output pairs. Hidden self-attention outputs are activations A∈R^{L×R×d}. The comparison metric (activation similarity / asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, yielding shape L×R. The studied sequences compare T=[I∘X] with demonstrations versus T=X without them under different weights.

Section 3 argues V2K and Q7M are not practically the same: although V2K responses are more calibrated than Q7M at similar or slightly better output quality, the internal activations do not match across models, especially in middle layers. The section cites internal-gradient-descent interpretations to suggest that if Q7M were functionally equivalent to V2K, output-position activations would be similar, but the observed similarity pattern is instead higher in initial/final layers than in middle layers. Figure 2 compares layerwise similarity (K4X) to V2K activations: H9C shows low similarity, while P4Z aligns much more closely and performs better. The experiment collects A_V2K on 100 test samples from multiple datasets (including B7V and W3F) using T=[I∘X], then trains on the same demonstrations to convergence and collects A_Q7M using T=X. Models span Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 with 1B/16-layer, 3B/28-layer, and 4B/36-layer correspondences; output-position similarity is K4X(A_V2K, A_Q7M).

Section 4 introduces R8D = IA2, a priming method meant to align layerwise processing rather than output similarity. It seeks adapted Q/K/V/O weights so that SA([I∘X]; W_QKVO) ≈ SA(X; \tilde W_QKVO) for the newly generated token at index -1. The text says Chen et al. (2024a) provide a closed-form linearized-attention solution, but this paper aims for a practical nonlinear-transformer version. For each training sample X_i, it constructs I from the remaining dataset, generates \hat Y_i from [I∘X_i], and collects V2K output-position activations A^i_V2K for G response tokens. It then supplies [X_i∘\hat Y_i] to obtain unaligned output-position activations A^i and minimizes the MSE ||A^i - A^i_V2K|| until convergence.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. All methods/dataset combinations are trained up to 50 epochs at three learning rates, with the best learning rate selected; over 13,000 models were trained. Rank-8 LoRAs target SA matrices W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token runs are more expensive, so N is capped at 16 for Llama and 8 for Qwen. Activation collection uses G=200 by default, yielding \hat A_i \in R^{L\times 200\times d}; target-token training instead uses the ground-truth response length. Single-token evaluation uses first-token probabilities for accuracy (U6R) and calibration (D8P/ECE); base models with demonstrations are evaluated five times and averaged, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations. Multi-token evaluation only considers correctly answered, correctly formatted outputs and does not measure calibration. Qwen3-4B-Base is used on all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B is used for all single-token tasks except E2T (which needs Llama-3.2-3B because 1B stays near random), and multi-token experiments use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Tasks include sentiment, StrategyQA, AGNews/BBCNews, MCQ with remapped option tokens (E2T from SciQ and G6A from QASC), GSM8K/GSM Symbolic, MATH Algebra, and SciQ. Few-shot training uses N in powers of two with five random sets per N and shared training data across methods. Multi-token outputs use chain-of-thought style parsing; L9S/X4C require the exact numerical answer after '####', V7B uses \boxed{}, and O3D uses support text plus exact text-answer matching. Section 5.1 reports that one method outperforms another in most single-token cases on accuracy and calibration, with another often matching V2K-like calibration without target-response-token training.

The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

Paper title: "IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations" (subtitle: "Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning." Authors: Aayush Mishra, Daniel Khashabi, Anqi Liu, JHU). Abstract claims that across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, IA2 significantly improves output quality and calibration, offering practical adaptation and insight into internal mechanics. It also says R8D is self-distillation that replicates V2K activation patterns in weight-trained models to incentivize V2K-like internal reasoning, and that its priming signal is unavailable through H9C. Introduction motivation: generic LLMs are used for specialized applications; PEFT is efficient; supervised generalization typically needs many labeled samples; demonstrations/instructions use context budget and inference compute. Main research question: whether information-rich V2K activations can improve Q7M quality. The hypothesis is that these activations encode generalizable contextual patterns that may be absent from few-shot weight adaptation, which can overfit shortcuts or targets. The paper argues matching outputs alone does not guarantee matching internal functioning. Figure 1 frames standard Q7M as output-space agreement between response and target and says it tends to be subpar and miscalibrated under low data; the proposed pipeline instead collects V2K activations, enforces functional alignment, then trains against target responses.

Paper title: "IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations" (subtitle: "Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning." Authors: Aayush Mishra, Daniel Khashabi, Anqi Liu, JHU). Abstract claims that across 12 benchmarks and two model families, IA2 improves output quality and calibration, and that R8D self-distills V2K activation patterns into weight-trained models to encourage V2K-like internal reasoning; its priming signal is unavailable through H9C. Introduction: the paper asks whether information-rich V2K activations can improve Q7M quality, arguing weight adaptation may overfit shortcuts while matching outputs does not ensure matching internal functioning. Figure 1 contrasts standard Q7M output-space agreement with a proposed pipeline that collects V2K activations, enforces functional alignment, then trains against target responses.

Background/notation: task data D_T={ (X_i,Y_i) }_{i=1}^N. Q7M/SFT updates weights Θ→Θ' so M_{Θ'}(X_t)=\bar y_t, the first token of \bar Y_t, with autoregressive continuation generating the full response. Training loss sums cross-entropy over G generated tokens. The decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers; SA is defined with W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O and causal prefix tokens t_{:i}. V2K/ICL uses concatenated demonstrations I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] and produces M_Θ(I∘X_t)=\hat y_t without weight updates; the setting here uses classic input–output pairs. Hidden self-attention outputs are activations A∈R^{L×R×d}. The comparison metric (activation similarity / asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors, yielding shape L×R. The studied sequences compare T=[I∘X] with demonstrations versus T=X without them under different weights.

Section 3 argues V2K and Q7M are not practically the same: although V2K responses are more calibrated than Q7M at similar or slightly better output quality, the internal activations do not match across models, especially in middle layers. The section cites internal-gradient-descent interpretations to suggest that if Q7M were functionally equivalent to V2K, output-position activations would be similar, but the observed similarity pattern is instead higher in initial/final layers than in middle layers. Figure 2 compares layerwise similarity (K4X) to V2K activations: H9C shows low similarity, while P4Z aligns much more closely and performs better. The experiment collects A_V2K on 100 test samples from multiple datasets (including B7V and W3F) using T=[I∘X], then trains on the same demonstrations to convergence and collects A_Q7M using T=X. Models span Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 with 1B/16-layer, 3B/28-layer, and 4B/36-layer correspondences; output-position similarity is K4X(A_V2K, A_Q7M).

Section 4 introduces R8D = IA2, a priming method meant to align layerwise processing rather than output similarity. It seeks adapted Q/K/V/O weights so that SA([I∘X]; W_QKVO) ≈ SA(X; \tilde W_QKVO) for the newly generated token at index -1. The text says Chen et al. (2024a) provide a closed-form linearized-attention solution, but this paper aims for a practical nonlinear-transformer version. For each training sample X_i, it constructs I from the remaining dataset, generates \hat Y_i from [I∘X_i], and collects V2K output-position activations A^i_V2K for G response tokens. It then supplies [X_i∘\hat Y_i] to obtain unaligned output-position activations A^i and minimizes the MSE ||A^i - A^i_V2K|| until convergence.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. All methods/dataset combinations are trained up to 50 epochs at three learning rates, with the best learning rate selected; over 13,000 models were trained. Rank-8 LoRAs target SA matrices W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token runs are more expensive, so N is capped at 16 for Llama and 8 for Qwen. Activation collection uses G=200 by default, yielding \hat A_i \in R^{L\times 200\times d}; target-token training instead uses the ground-truth response length. Single-token evaluation uses first-token probabilities for accuracy (U6R) and calibration (D8P/ECE); base models with demonstrations are evaluated five times and averaged, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations. Multi-token evaluation only considers correctly answered, correctly formatted outputs and does not measure calibration. Qwen3-4B-Base is used on all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B is used for all single-token tasks except E2T (which needs Llama-3.2-3B because 1B stays near random), and multi-token experiments use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Tasks include sentiment, StrategyQA, AGNews/BBCNews, MCQ with remapped option tokens (E2T from SciQ and G6A from QASC), GSM8K/GSM Symbolic, MATH Algebra, and SciQ. Few-shot training uses N in powers of two with five random sets per N and shared training data across methods. Multi-token outputs use chain-of-thought style parsing; L9S/X4C require the exact numerical answer after '####', V7B uses \boxed{}, and O3D uses support text plus exact text-answer matching. Section 5.1 reports that one method outperforms another in most single-token cases on accuracy and calibration, with another often matching V2K-like calibration without target-response-token training.

Table 1 (Qwen3-4B-Base, N=4) reports single-token results for eval methods V2K, H9C, J3N, and P4Z. Across the shown source rows, P4Z often has the best U6R, but calibration (D8P, lower is better) is mixed: it is not always best and can be worse than other methods on some rows. Table 2 (same model, N=4) reports multi-token U6R only; P4Z is better than H9C on every row, but sometimes below V2K. Section 5.2 argues H9C updates are almost orthogonal to other methods, while the best P4Z models share substantial spanned weight space with J3N (about 39%). It attributes P4Z’s gains to R8D/priming: baseline = H9C (SFT only), J3N = IA2 only, P4Z = IA2→SFT. It also says priming raises K4X, sequential adaptation keeps it elevated, and P4Z sits between the other conditions on K4X while improving U6R and calibration.

Figure 3 plots K4X(A, A_V2K) versus U6R/D8P for one training experiment per point. It reports that D8P decreases smoothly as similarity increases, and that even extreme alignment can still leave some U6R gains obtainable from ground-truth training. The section argues that unchanged base weights substantially affect activations under LoRA, so activation patterns alone cannot isolate training-induced behavioral changes. Instead, it proposes direct weight analysis across all single- and multi-token experiments, using SVD basis vectors and a subspace-overlap measure A5Y = (1/r)||U1^T U2||_F^2 to quantify shared weight space and compare methods.

The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

final_notes: Section 8 concludes that the paper’s main finding is a mechanistic distinction between ICL and SFT: they adapt via different mechanisms, and ICL often captures richer, more generalizable patterns. The paper introduces IA2 as an SFT priming technique that induces ICL-like internal behavior and moves models into a more adaptable weight subspace not reachable by SFT alone. The reported experimental takeaway is that IA2 improves both accuracy and calibration of SFT. Future work proposed in the conclusion includes evaluating IA2’s effects on diversity and catastrophic forgetting in IA2-based SFT, and studying IA2 on post-trained (RL-tuned) models. The final reproducibility statement says the authors provide code and that the paper’s details plus a README should allow full reproduction with repeatable random seeds.

Section 3 argues V2K and Q7M are not practically the same: although V2K responses are more calibrated than Q7M at similar or slightly better output quality, the internal activations do not match across models, especially in middle layers. The paper studies whether internal computations from in-context learning (ICL) can improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It proposes ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), which trains a model without demonstrations to match its own activations with demonstrations, then fine-tunes on ground-truth responses. The paper claims experiments on 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings: IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration; IA2 and SFT identify different weight subspaces; IA2-based training does not consistently beat ICL, especially on some multi-token math tasks. The paper also examines simultaneous IA2+SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method.

This part is a glossary/notation section. It defines the main adaptation settings: SFT, ICL, IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment), priming, IA2→SFT, and IA2+SFT. IA2 is described as self-distillation where a model without demonstrations matches activations from ICL demonstrations, using an ICL-conditioned teacher and a student trained from those signals. It also defines the main evaluation settings and task families used later: single-token vs multi-token, exact match parsing, calibration/ECE, in-distribution vs OOD, and the specific datasets/tasks (SST2, FinS, PoemS, StrategyQA, AGNews, BBCNews, SciQ/QASC, GSM8K/GSM8Ks, MATH Algebra). The section also records the model families (Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 variants), PEFT methods (LoRA, (IA)3), and key equations/notation for attention, activation matching, loss terms, subspace overlap, and parsing formats.

This section is the paper title and abstract. It frames IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) as a self-distillation method that matches ICL activations before SFT, using the model’s own ICL processing as a teacher to encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. The abstract claims ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns and that IA2 used as a priming step before SFT improves both accuracy and calibration (ECE) across 12 benchmarks and two model families. It highlights example gains on FinS (accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7; ECE 0.31 vs 0.16) and HMathA (accuracy 50.4 vs 55.3). The section also states the work covers 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, later identified as Qwen3 and Llama-3.2.

The introduction contrasts ICL and SFT on cost, calibration, and internal processing. SFT is described as requiring labeled data and typically needing many samples, while ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference time, often generalizes well in few-shot settings, and is usually well calibrated but consumes context space. The paper argues that although ICL and SFT can produce similar outputs, their internal activations differ, indicating different adaptation mechanisms. IA2 is introduced as a method that uses ICL activations as a teacher signal to align a model’s internal behavior with its own ICL processing before SFT. The pipeline is: collect rich ICL activations, enforce functional alignment with ICL, then perform SFT on the primed model. The introduction claims this priming step improves text classification and generation performance, that the IA2 training signal is unavailable from SFT-only training, and that the authors trained over 13,000 models across 12 benchmarks. Figure 1 is described as contrasting standard output-space-only SFT with IA2’s functional alignment approach.

Section 2 defines the model and notation. A decoder-only transformer LM \(M_\Theta\) has self-attention and linear layers over token vectors \(T=[t_i]_{i=1}^R\), with the final token’s projection fed to the LM head. Self-attention is written with \(W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O\) and outputs \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}\); it uses causal context \(t_{:i}\) for token \(i\). SFT uses a dataset of input-output pairs \(\mathcal D_\mathcal T\), updates \(\Theta\to\Theta'\), and trains by cross-entropy over generated response tokens. ICL uses concatenated demonstrations \(I=[X_1\circ Y_1\circ\dots\circ X_n\circ Y_n]\) plus a new test input \(X_t\), with no weight updates, and produces an output \(\hat Y_t\). The paper restricts attention to classic ICL with input-output demonstrations, though it notes instructions can be viewed as a form of ICL in frontier models. Activations are defined as hidden self-attention outputs; a model with \(L\) layers and \(R\) tokens yields an activation tensor \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times R\times d}\). The paper compares activations for prompts with ICL \((T=[I\circ X])\) versus without ICL \((T=X)\), and defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\).

Section 3 argues that ICL and SFT are not internally equivalent. It motivates the comparison via prior claims that ICL behaves like internal gradient descent, which would imply similar activations between a prompt with demonstrations and an SFT model without demonstrations. The authors test this by collecting ICL activations A_ICL for 100 test samples from SST2, AGNews, and other datasets, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models with 16, 28, and 36 layers. They train SFT models on the same demonstrations to convergence, collect A_SFT on X without demonstrations, and compute token-level cosine similarity (asim) at output-token positions, averaged across tokens, samples, and datasets. The reported result is that ICL and SFT activations are different, with better alignment near early and late layers and worse alignment in the middle layers. The section also says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar or slightly better accuracy, and concludes that SFT should not be expected to replace ICL directly. It then motivates the next question: whether ICL-like activations can be used to improve SFT, leading into the next section.

Section 4 proposes IA2, a two-step method to induce ICL-like behavior in SFT models. First, it aims to align attention weights ~W_QKVO so that the model processes inputs like it does under ICL, using the approximation SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;~W) for all task inputs. For each training sample X_i, the method generates an ICL response ˆY_i from [I∘X_i], collects output-position activations A_ICL^i ∈ R^{L×G×d}, then feeds [X_i∘ˆY_i] without demonstrations and trains to match activations via an MSE-style loss. Second, after IA2, it continues with standard SFT on ground-truth targets Y_i, retraining from the IA2-aligned weights. The section claims IA2 followed by SFT improves adaptation over SFT alone, citing FinS→FinS accuracy 78.7 vs 67.4 and ECE 0.16 vs 0.31, and GSM8K accuracy 68.8 vs 64.5.

Section 5 describes the experimental setup. The paper studies single-token and multi-token adaptation tasks, using the same training data for compared methods and also evaluating OOD transfer. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), True/False (StrategyQA), news categorization (AGNews, BBCNews), and MCQ tasks (SciQ/QASC remapped to SciQr/QASCr). Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and SciQ in a generation setting. Training datasets use few-shot sizes N in powers of 2 (e.g., 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), with 5 random sets per N, and IA2 uses the other N−1 samples as demonstrations to form A_ICL. Evaluation uses a separate 500-example sample per task. For multi-token tasks, outputs are chain-of-thought style text, with dataset-specific parsing; exact answer matching is used. The main models are Qwen3-4B-Base for all tasks, Llama-3.2-1B for most single-token tasks, Llama-3.2-3B for SciQr, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for multi-token secondary experiments. Training uses rank-8 LoRAs on W_Q, W_K, and W_O. Multi-token experiments cap generated tokens at G=200; SFT uses the ground-truth answer length. Each method–dataset pair is trained up to 50 epochs with three learning rates, selecting the best rate. Single-token evaluation reports accuracy and ECE from the first-token distribution. Base-model ICL is benchmarked by averaging over 5 different demonstration sets, while trained methods are evaluated without demonstrations.

final_notes: Section 7.4 frames adversarial transferability in VLMs as trade-offs: CroPA optimizes against competing text embeddings, aiding cross-prompt transfer but tying perturbations to a specific model architecture and image-specific features, which limits cross-model and cross-image generalization. D-UAP targets more generalizable vision-encoder components and improves cross-model transfer more for architecturally similar models (e.g., BLIP-2/InstructBLIP) than for different ones (e.g., BLIP-2/Flamingo). SCMix and CutMix are proposed to improve cross-image transfer, but they do not fully resolve the cross-prompt vs cross-image tension. Diffusion-based initialization is described as improving ASR while preserving cross-prompt transferability, though the paper argues no method can maximize all transferability dimensions at once. Section 7.5 says high cross-prompt transferability is a security risk for attackers, but imperceptible perturbations could also be used defensively to force non-sensitive outputs and protect private information. The paper also says it introduces refinements to CroPA, including improved initialization and an enhanced loss function, which increase ASR and generalizability across models and images. Section 7.6 says the reproduction succeeded on key CroPA results and ablations, but resource limits constrained larger-scale cross-model and ensemble experiments. Section 7.7 reports no direct communication with the original authors, and an unresolved GitHub issue about BLIP-2/InstructBLIP remains open.

Section 5.1 proposes replacing CroPA’s random noise initialization with a semantically informed initialization. The idea is to synthesize a target image from a prompt using a diffusion model (e.g., SDXL), then align the adversarial perturbation with the target image’s vision-encoder features via an MSE-based objective. They claim this can improve attack efficacy, convergence speed, visual fidelity, and cross-prompt transferability. Preliminary experiments on BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP reportedly show better efficacy than random initialization with only about 20–25 seconds extra computation per image. Section 7 discusses the paper’s replication and interpretation of Luo et al. (2024). It claims the authors substantiated CroPA’s strong cross-prompt transferability and few-shot robustness. It also argues the new semantically informed noise initialization (diffusion-synthesized reference image plus feature-space alignment) outperforms CroPA and random initialization, improving targeted ASR and reducing optimization steps. For cross-image transferability, the paper says CroPA is limited to image-specific low-level features, and that SCMix and CutMix improve transfer, with SCMix giving the larger gain. For cross-model transferability, the paper says D-UAP-modified CroPA achieves 96.85% overall targeted ASR, a 13.5% improvement over base CroPA, with especially strong gains on VQA-general and captioning, including on harmful targets like “Bomb.” It claims transfer is better between models with similar vision encoders, but still limited by dependency on the specific vision encoder.

Section 7.4 frames adversarial transferability in VLMs as trade-offs. It says CroPA optimizes against competing text embeddings, which helps cross-prompt transfer but ties perturbations to a specific model architecture and image-specific features, limiting cross-model and cross-image generalization. The D-UAP enhancement targets more generalizable vision-encoder components; it improves cross-model transfer more for architecturally similar models (e.g., BLIP-2/InstructBLIP) than for different ones (e.g., BLIP-2/Flamingo). SCMix and CutMix are proposed to improve cross-image transfer, but they do not fully solve the cross-prompt vs cross-image tension. The diffusion-based initialization is described as improving ASR while preserving cross-prompt transferability, though the paper still argues no method can maximize all transferability dimensions at once. Section 7.5 says high cross-prompt transferability is a security risk for attackers, but imperceptible perturbations could also be used defensively to force non-sensitive outputs and protect private information. The paper also says it introduces refinements to CroPA, including improved initialization and an enhanced loss function, which increase ASR and generalizability across models and images.

final_notes: Section 7.4 argues there are trade-offs among cross-prompt, cross-model, and cross-image transferability. CroPA is strong for cross-prompt transfer but weaker across models/images. D-UAP improves cross-model transfer modestly for similar architectures (e.g., BLIP-2 vs. InstructBLIP) but less for different ones (e.g., BLIP-2 vs. Flamingo). SCMix/CutMix improve cross-image transfer but do not remove the trade-off, and diffusion-based initialization can raise ASR without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability, though a broader tension remains. Section 7.5 says the methods increase ASR and generalizability across models and images, and that cross-prompt attacks can be both offensive and privacy-protective. The conclusion says the reproducibility study affirms Luo et al. (2024) but highlights the need for deeper study of cross-prompt adversarial transferability. Limitations: resource constraints limited experiments on large VLMs (Flamingo, BLIP-2), broader cross-model evaluation, and ensemble-based analysis. Future work should improve cross-model transferability, develop encoder-agnostic methods, enhance cross-image generalization, and explore query-based optimization.

It states the authors reproduce and verify four main claims of the original CroPA paper: (1) CroPA achieves cross-prompt transferability across various target texts and outperforms baselines, independent of semantic meaning or word frequency; (2) CroPA has the best overall performance across different numbers of prompts, with rapid convergence but baselines still not surpassing CroPA; (3) CroPA converges toward higher ASR as attack iterations increase; (4) CroPA outperforms baselines under few-shot/in-context learning settings. Section 4 formalizes CroPA for VLMs. Inputs are visual x_v and textual x_t; adversarial image perturbation δ_v is bounded by ||δ_v||_p ≤ ε_v. Two attack settings are defined: targeted attack minimizes language modeling loss toward a target text T over k prompts (Eq. 1), while non-targeted attack maximizes discrepancy between clean and adversarial outputs (Eq. 2). Baselines are Single-P (single prompt, Eq. 3) and Multi-P (multiple prompts, Eq. 4). CroPA uses both image and prompt perturbations with opposing objectives: min_{δ_v} max_{δ_t} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T) (Eq. 5). The method is implemented via PGD with iterative updates; image updates use gradient descent, prompt updates use gradient ascent, and the prompt-update interval is controlled by N. Algorithm 1 initializes x'_v = x_v, samples prompts from X_t, and updates x'_v each step; the rest of the algorithm continues beyond the current excerpt.

Section 4’s Algorithm 1 continues: it computes the gradient for the adversarial prompt, updates the prompt by gradient ascent when the prompt-update condition holds, then projects the image perturbation back into the ε-ball around the original image and returns x'_v. The paper states that during evaluation only the optimized image perturbation is applied and prompt perturbations are discarded, so the attack’s effectiveness is attributed to the image perturbation’s transferability rather than prompt changes.

Section 5 argues that CroPA’s PGD-based optimization is effective on a single model but has limited transferability, and that Table 1 shows poor performance on some tasks (especially classification and captioning). It also claims CroPA is computationally heavy: over 6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images. The authors motivate extended experiments to improve task consistency and transferability, especially across images and models.

Section 5.1 proposes Noise Initialization via Vision Encoding Optimization: instead of random noise initialization, they suggest semantically informed initialization using a diffusion model and the vision encoder feature space. They claim this should improve convergence, attack efficacy, and cross-prompt transferability while preserving imperceptibility. Preliminary experiments on BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP are said to show better efficacy than random initialization, with only 20–25 seconds extra per image on one GPU.

Section 5.1.2 defines diffusion-based target synthesis with Stable Diffusion XL to generate a target image x_target from a prompt T.

Section 5.1.2 says the target image x_target is generated from a prompt T by a Stable Diffusion XL diffusion process; x_target is described as capturing the semantic essence of T. Section 5.1.3 defines the initial perturbation by minimizing the squared L2 distance between vision-encoder outputs f_v(x+δ) and f_v(x_target), subject to an l_infty bound ||δ||_∞ <= ε. Section 5.1.4 then refines the adversarial example with PGD using MSE between f_v(x_adv) and f_v(x_target) as the loss.

Section 5.2 argues CroPA is weak because it treats image and text modalities uniformly and does not exploit the vision encoder’s representational backbone; it claims CroPA perturbations lack targeted influence on the encoder and therefore have limited transferability. The proposed fix is to combine CroPA with a perturbation loss that disrupts the vision encoder’s attention value vectors, inspired by Doubly-UAP. The authors say they will freeze the text encoder, optimize CroPA loss plus a modified Doubly-UAP loss, and aim to improve ASR and cross-model robustness while keeping CroPA-like hyperparameter constraints. The section ends by saying they will focus on two attention components with fundamental roles, but does not yet specify them.

Section 5.2 now specifies the two attention components mentioned earlier: (1) attention weights, which govern inter-patch interactions, and (2) value vectors, which contain the patch information. The paper says it targets the vision encoder’s attention mechanism, especially the value vectors in the middle-to-late layers, as the most vulnerable components. It recalls standard Doubly-UAP, where a perturbation maximizes loss between value vectors of x and x+δ across layers. The modified approach introduces a target value vector from a reference image associated with target text T, uses cosine-similarity-based loss between perturbed value vectors and this target, and combines it with CroPA in the final objective: L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t, T) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v). The authors claim this should preserve adversariality while adding semantic alignment, but may transfer best only to models with similar vision encoders. Section 5.3 begins a new discussion of cross-image transferability via image augmentation, noting that CroPA is learned for a single image across prompts and introducing UAPs and CutMix as relevant prior work.

Section 5.3 expands prior work on transferability with ETU, which uses SCMix (self-mix + cross-mix) to improve cross-image transferability; the paper says it adopts SCMix because, for the same model, SCMix alone performs better than ETU’s full method with local utility reinforcement. SCMix is described as a two-stage augmentation: self-mixing of a base image I1 via random crops/resizing and fixed η=0.5, followed by cross-mixing with a secondary image I2 using β1 >> β2 so I1’s semantics remain dominant and aligned with text T1. The authors argue this regularizes against overfitting and can promote universal perturbations that are both cross-prompt and cross-image transferable. CutMix is presented as another augmentation baseline that replaces rectangular regions via a binary mask, encouraging spatially invariant features. Section 5.4 then defines the transferability threat model: the attacker has white-box access to a surrogate model (BLIP-2 or Flamingo in experiments), only architectural knowledge of target models, and an L∞ budget ε=16/255, with cross-model settings to be detailed next.

Then S3D refinement minimizes squared encoder distance to x_target under projection back to the ε-ball. Section 5.2 says value vectors in middle-to-late vision layers are vulnerable; X9C / D-UAP is adapted by minimizing, rather than maximizing, losses between value vectors of x_i and T_i.

Section 5.2 argues that attacking vision-output embeddings can impair LVLM perception because attention weights govern patch interactions and value vectors carry the patch information. It proposes an X9C-style objective on middle-to-late-layer value vectors and a combined method P2F (CroPA+D-UAP / re-CroPA) that uses target-associated reference-image value vectors, cosine-similarity loss, and the Q7X objective together, with a possible transferability limit to models with similar vision encoders.

Section 5.3 studies transfer across images via augmentation because per-image iterative gradients overfit and are costly. It evaluates J6T (SCMix) and U8G (CutMix). J6T self-mixes two random crops/resizes of a base image, then cross-mixes with a second image; this implementation fixes η=0.5 (rather than sampling from Beta) to preserve dominant semantics while improving invariance. U8G uses a binary rectangle mask to replace a region from one image with another. J6T is preferred because, on the same model, it outperforms the version with additional local utility reinforcement.

final_notes:
Section 7.5 says high cross-prompt transferability can be harmful for attackers because adversarial images can induce misleading outputs under harmless queries, but it may also be useful for defense: imperceptible perturbations could make VLMs output predetermined non-sensitive text and help protect private images. The authors say their initialization and loss refinements improve ASR and generalization across models/images, strengthening cross-prompt attacks and possibly helping defenses. They conclude that cross-prompt transferability matters for robust VLMs, countermeasures, user-data protection, and output integrity.

Section 7.6 notes limitations: limited computation constrained experiment scale, tuning, architectural coverage, and ensemble evaluation. They reproduced key CroPA results but could not fully explore Flamingo/BLIP2-scale experiments, broader hyperparameter tuning, or ensembles. Future work: encoder-agnostic attacks, better cross-image generalization, and query-based optimization.

Section 7.7 says no direct communication with the original authors was established, and the BLIP-2/InstructBLIP GitHub issue remains unresolved.

steps.notes_before: Section 4 defines the attack setup and CroPA reproduction. The paper distinguishes targeted attacks (minimize loss to produce a fixed target text \(T\) across \(k\) prompts) from non-targeted attacks (maximize discrepancy between clean and adversarial outputs); ASR is exact-match for targeted and output-change for non-targeted. Baselines are Single-P (one prompt) and Multi-P (prompt set). CroPA is formulated as a min-max objective over image and prompt perturbations, with PGD-style updates: the image perturbation is updated by gradient descent, the prompt perturbation by gradient ascent, and prompt updates occur every \(N\) steps. Algorithm 1 returns only the adversarial image \(x_v'\); evaluation discards prompt perturbations and uses only the optimized image. Internal issue noted: the algorithm updates \(x_t'^{\,i}\) but computes gradients on \(x_t^i\), so the prompt perturbation never enters the forward pass.

Section 5 presents extensions aimed at inconsistent task performance and transferability (cross-image and cross-model), motivated by CroPA’s limited transferability and high compute cost. It claims CroPA takes over 6 hours to train perturbations for 50 images on a 48GB L40S GPU, using 95% VRAM. Section 5.1 proposes semantically informed noise initialization: use a diffusion model (Stable Diffusion XL) to synthesize a target image from the desired prompt, then optimize an initial perturbation to match the target image in the VLM vision encoder’s feature space via MSE under an l_infty bound. Subsection 5.1.1 says preliminary BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP tests show stronger attacks with only 20–25 seconds extra per image on one GPU, while preserving fidelity within the perturbation budget. Section 5.1.3 defines delta_init = argmin_{||delta||_inf<=epsilon} ||f_v(x+delta)-f_v(x_target)||_2^2. 5.1.4 begins adversarial refinement via PGD but no details are visible yet.

Section 5.2 proposes a transferability-oriented modification of CroPA that targets the vision encoder’s attention/value vectors, especially value vectors in middle-to-late layers, to improve ASR and cross-model transferability. The combined objective is written as \(L_{re-CroPA}=L_{CroPA}-\lambda L_{d-UAP}\), which appears sign-inconsistent with the accompanying description that says to minimize this loss.

Section 5.3 frames image augmentation as a way to improve CroPA’s cross-image transfer. It cites UAP work for VLP models, CutMix, and ETU/SCMix. SCMix is defined as two-stage augmentation: self-mixing two cropped/resized variants of a base image I1, then cross-mixing that result with a secondary image I2. The paper fixes the self-mix weight to eta=0.5, said to be equivalent to alpha=∞ in the original Beta(alpha,alpha) sampling. Cross-mixing uses I3 = beta1 I1' + beta2 I2 with beta1 >> beta2, preserving I1’s semantics while adding diversity. CutMix is defined as hard mask-based regional replacement: x~ = M⊙xA + (1-M)⊙xB. The section argues SCMix and CutMix reduce image-specific overfitting and may encourage spatially invariant, more transferable perturbations.

Section 5.4 begins the threat model for transferability experiments. For cross-model transfer, the attacker has white-box access to a surrogate model (BLIP-2 or Flamingo) and aims to generate one perturbation that makes multiple VLMs produce a specified target text regardless of prompt; target models are black-box, and the budget is ε=16/255 under L∞.

steps.notes_before:
The paper’s scope is to reproduce Luo et al. (2024) on CroPA and test four claims: (1) cross-prompt transfer across target texts, (2) best overall performance across prompt counts, (3) ASR improves with more iterations, and (4) CroPA beats baselines in few-shot settings. It also evaluates cross-model and cross-image effectiveness and compares CroPA with other cross-prompt methods.

Methodology: attacks are formulated for targeted and non-targeted settings over multiple prompts. The targeted objective minimizes loss toward a target text; the non-targeted objective maximizes discrepancy between clean and adversarial outputs. Baselines are Single-P (one prompt) and Multi-P (a prompt set), both originally from Luo et al. (2024). CroPA is described as a min-max PGD method where image perturbations minimize loss and prompt perturbations maximize it, with prompt updates occurring every N image updates. Algorithm 1 returns only the adversarial image \(x_v'\), and evaluation discards prompt perturbations.

Important inconsistency to check later: the algorithm updates \(x_t^{\prime i}\) but computes gradients using \(x_t^i\), so the updated prompt is not actually used in the loss.

Section 5 introduces extensions for three issues: inconsistent task performance, high computation cost, and limited transferability. It claims CroPA’s single-model loss feedback limits transferability; this is supported by Table 9 (Appendix A.1) and poor Classification/Captioning results in Table 1. It also reports CroPA is computationally intensive: training perturbations for 50 images takes over 6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU and uses 95% VRAM. steps.notes_before: Section 4 formalizes the attack setting for VLMs with visual input x_v and text input x_t under an ℓ_p-bounded image perturbation δ_v. It distinguishes targeted attacks (optimize toward a specified target text T across multiple prompts) and non-targeted attacks (maximize the discrepancy between clean and adversarial outputs). Baselines introduced from Luo et al. (2024) are Single-P (optimize one prompt) and Multi-P (optimize over multiple prompts), with analogous targeted/non-targeted versions. CroPA uses both image perturbation δ_v and learnable prompt perturbation δ_t in a min-max objective: δ_v minimizes language-model loss while δ_t maximizes it. The method is implemented with iterative PGD-style updates and a configurable prompt-update interval N.

Section 4 formalizes the attack setting for VLMs with visual input x_v and text input x_t under an ℓ_p-bounded image perturbation δ_v. It distinguishes targeted attacks (optimize toward a specified target text T across multiple prompts) and non-targeted attacks (maximize the discrepancy between clean and adversarial outputs). Baselines from Luo et al. (2024) are Single-P (optimize one prompt) and Multi-P (optimize over multiple prompts), with analogous targeted/non-targeted versions. CroPA uses both image perturbation δ_v and learnable prompt perturbation δ_t in a min-max objective: δ_v minimizes language-model loss while δ_t maximizes it. The method uses iterative PGD-style updates, with prompt updates performed at a configurable interval N. The algorithm computes gradients for adversarial prompts via ascent updates, projects the image perturbation back into the ε-ball, returns the optimized image perturbation, and discards prompt perturbations during evaluation.

Section 5 argues that CroPA’s PGD-based optimization is effective on a single model but has limited transferability and is computationally expensive (over 6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images). The authors frame their extended experiments as addressing CroPA’s inconsistent performance across tasks and improving image-perturbation transferability (cross-image and cross-model). Section 5.1 proposes replacing CroPA’s random noise initialization with a semantically informed initialization. The idea is to synthesize a target image from a prompt using a diffusion model (e.g., SDXL), then align the adversarial perturbation with the target image’s vision-encoder features via an MSE-based objective. They claim this can improve attack efficacy, convergence speed, visual fidelity, and cross-prompt transferability. final_notes:
Section 7 discusses reproducibility, transferability trade-offs, broader impact, and limitations. Reproduction used the authors’ public repository and original configurations, but BLIP-2 and InstructBLIP produced runtime errors and needed debugging. The discussion says semantic initialization generally outperforms Q7X and random baselines; gradients already capture some target context, and initialization gives only a modest Y2K gain but helps convergence toward adversarial directions.

For K3R, J6T improves transfer especially for VQA, T4B, and D5R, while U8G also improves over the base image-transfer version; augmentation helps cross-image generalization but does not remove the limitation. For F8V, X9C is framed as robust to harmful target text and guardrail activation, but encoder-specific dependence still limits heterogeneous-architecture transfer; it is presented as progress toward more universal attacks. The discussion emphasizes trade-offs: N6Z and F8V/K3R are competing objectives, and no single method maximizes all transfer forms simultaneously. Semantic anchoring can raise H2Q without sacrificing N6Z, but optimization for one transfer dimension can reduce another.

Broader impact notes that strong N6Z can enable misinformation or subversion, while imperceptible perturbations may also be used for privacy protection. Limitations include GPU/memory scarcity, especially for Flamingo and BLIP-2, which constrained large-scale evaluation, tuning, and broader architecture testing. Future work includes ensemble-model transfer, encoder-agnostic F8V, stronger K3R, and query-based optimization. No direct communication with the original authors occurred; the BLIP-2/InstructBLIP GitHub issue remained unresolved.

Paper title: "Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models." Authors from IIT Roorkee. Abstract claims the reproducibility study validates the original CroPA paper ("An Image is Worth 1000 Lies: Adversarial Transferability Across Prompts on Vision-Language Models") and its superiority to existing baselines; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability. It also claims proposed enhancements: initialization, common perturbations across images, and attention-directed loss. Evaluations cover Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and extended LLaVA experiments. The abstract says original results are validated and enhancements consistently improve adversarial effectiveness.

Paper studies reproducibility of CroPA (“An Image is Worth 1000 Lies: Adversarial Transferability Across Prompts on Vision-Language Models”) and proposes enhancements. Introduction frames three transfer settings: cross-model transferability, cross-image transferability, and cross-prompt transferability; it says cross-image transferability corresponds to universal adversarial perturbations shared across images. Related work cited includes attacks on BLIP/BLIP-2, white-box targeted/untargeted attacks, harmful instruction-following attacks, and multimodal attack evaluations. The paper says its replication examines superiority across target texts, saturation with more prompts, robustness with in-context examples, convergence over iterations, and taskwise analysis beyond aggregate results. Proposed extensions include initialization improving both some attack metric (H2Q) and transferability, shared perturbations with transfer-promoting image augmentation, and attention/value-based targeted manipulation to improve generalization and H2Q.

The paper’s related-work section situates adversarial transferability across three dimensions: cross-task, cross-model, and cross-image/generalized perturbations. It distinguishes early VLM attacks on lightweight CNN–RNN systems from newer black-box attacks on large VLMs such as BLIP/BLIP-2. For cross-prompt adversarial transferability, it says the area is still new, with no established benchmarks/baselines, but cites Yang et al. (2024) as an additional comparator (CIA / Contextual Injection Attack) and contrasts it with Luo et al. (2024)’s competing-prompt optimization. It also motivates transferability improvements via gradient misalignment, input diversity, and augmentation, which feed into the paper’s proposed enhancements.

The paper’s reproducibility scope for Luo et al. (2024) is defined around four named claims: (1) Q7X achieves N6Z across target texts, (2) Q7X has the best aggregate performance across prompt counts, (3) Q7X converges toward higher H2Q with increasing iterations, and (4) Q7X outperforms baselines in few-shot settings. Beyond faithful reproduction, the extended scope evaluates F8V, K3R, and comparison to other N6Z methods, testing whether images generated through Q7X maintain deceptive transfer across diverse VLMs, prompts, and model parameters. This section frames the work as assessing broader robustness and versatility of the attack, not just reproducing the original prompt-transfer improvement.

final_notes:
Section 7 concludes that cross-prompt transferability has both attack and defense implications: adversarial images can induce malicious outputs from harmless prompts, while perturbations could also force predetermined non-sensitive outputs to protect private images. It reiterates that initialization and loss refinements improve ASR and generalization across models/images and strengthen cross-prompt attacks. The paper’s closing synthesis claims the reproduction affirms Luo et al.’s foundation and underscores the importance of cross-prompt transferability for robust VLMs, countermeasures, user-data protection, and output integrity.

Section 7.6 says limited computation constrained experiment scale, hyperparameter tuning, architectural coverage, and ensemble evaluation; large VLM attacks (e.g., Flamingo, BLIP2) required substantial GPU memory/processing. Future work: encoder-agnostic attacks, better cross-image generalization, and query-based optimization.

Section 7.7 states no direct contact with the original authors and that the GitHub issue about BLIP-2/InstructBLIP remains unresolved.

Final claims-and-evidence summary for Section 7: CroPA supports cross-prompt and few-shot performance (Table 1; Table 2 shot=2 Overall 0.6635 vs Multi-P 0.5730). Initialization, augmentation, and value-vector guidance improve metrics: Table 4 CroPA+Init Overall 0.9209 vs CroPA 0.7958; Table 5 SCMix 0.7055 and CutMix 0.5565 vs base 0.4355; Table 6 CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 vs 0.8433; Table 8 cross-model rows. Trade-offs and encoder dependence remain important.

Related work frames adversarial transferability along model, image, and task dimensions. For VLMs, earlier attacks were mostly task-specific (captioning and VQA) and targeted lightweight CNN-RNN systems without in-context learning, limiting relevance to modern prompt-based VLMs. Zhao et al. Section 5.3 frames image augmentation as a way to improve CroPA’s cross-image transfer. It cites UAP work for VLP models, CutMix, and ETU/SCMix. SCMix is defined as two-stage augmentation: self-mixing two cropped/resized variants of a base image I1, then cross-mixing that result with a secondary image I2. The paper fixes the self-mix weight to eta=0.5, said to be equivalent to alpha=∞ in the original Beta(alpha,alpha) sampling. Cross-mixing uses I3 = beta1 I1' + beta2 I2 with beta1 >> beta2, preserving I1’s semantics while adding diversity. CutMix is defined as hard mask-based regional replacement: x~ = M⊙xA + (1-M)⊙xB.
