Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

The paper sets up two regimes: unrestricted Borel function classes, where Fisher consistency is the classical notion, and parametric but potentially mis-specified classes, where aggregation is claimed to improve consistency. It defines a distribution-dependent task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(.|X))], with the zero-one loss as a special case, and also an ordinary instantaneous task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)]. Surrogate methods replace the task loss by R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)], and the paper will study consistency of such replacements.

Label aggregation is introduced via an aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))], where Z is a response replacement and A is an aggregation map. Two examples are given: repeated labeling, where Z=(Y1,…,Ym) are iid labels for the same X and A(Z) is the empirical risk minimizer over labels (majority vote for zero-one loss), and a rough K-nearest-neighbor construction, where Z includes one query point and m additional iid samples and A_{m,K} predicts by minimizing loss over the K nearest labels. The setup also notes that the repeated-sampling framework extends to aggregation from a single sample in the appendix.

It then lists future directions: (i) finite-m consistency theory, especially for ranking in Sec. 3.1 and possibly higher-order comparisons; (ii) understanding the noise condition number κ(X) for multiclass problems and how it interacts with the loss/surrogate pair; (iii) extending results to mis-specified models beyond the “optimal predictability” assumption that a Bayes-optimal classifier lies in F; and (iv) restricted-class comparison inequalities / H-consistency with aggregation, with a note that quadratic growth of ψ is rate-optimal for smooth convex loss and aggregation might improve consistency in that setting.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated/cleaned labels have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning. Specifically: (1) in risk consistency settings, minimizing surrogate losses with label aggregation gives stronger consistency guarantees than possible with raw labels; (2) even when models are perfectly specified, standard approaches can fail if the loss is slightly mis-specified, but methods using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers for every fixed label count. The abstract frames this as showing robustness across the data pipeline from collection to prediction.

Introduction frames label cleaning/aggregation as a source of robustness unavailable without aggregation. Main claims: (1) for surrogate-loss minimization in risk consistency, using aggregated labels can achieve consistency and optimal prediction where raw-label procedures cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional settings, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. The paper contrasts standard $(X,Y)$-pair theory with modern data collection pipelines that involve multiple labels and denoising. It proposes examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where methods using only $(X,Y)$ fail but aggregation succeeds. It also promises new theory for surrogate consistency with aggregated labels, including nonparametric results relating number of aggregated samples and noise, approximate linear comparison inequalities for losses with aggregated labels, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes where standard theory may fail.

Section 2 sets up standard surrogate-risk minimization. Data $(X_i,Y_i)$ are i.i.d. from $P$; a scorer $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is decoded by $\mathsf d$ to predict $\hat y=\mathsf d\circ f(x)$. The task risk is $R(f)=\mathbb E_P[\ell(\mathsf d\circ f(X),Y)]$ (Eq. 1). The paper then shifts to a slightly more general risk that can depend on the conditional label distribution $P(Y\in\cdot\mid X)$ (Eq. 2), and introduces surrogate risk $R_\varphi(f)=\mathbb E_P[\varphi(f(X),Y)]$. The two consistency settings of interest are Fisher consistency with all Borel functions and parametric/misspecified hypothesis classes.

Label aggregation replaces the raw output $Y$ by $Z\in\mathcal Z$ and applies an aggregation map $A:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal A$, giving aggregated surrogate risk $R_{\varphi,A}(f)=\mathbb E[\varphi(f(X),A(Z))]$ (Eq. 3). Example 1: repeated labels $Z=(Y_1,\dots,Y_m)$ with majority-vote-style aggregation $A(Z)=\arg\min_y\sum_{l=1}^m \ell(y,Y_l)$; for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. Example 2: a $K$-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation using an extra sample $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m$ and labels of the $K$ nearest neighbors. The section says Appendix C extends these population-level aggregation ideas to a single-sample setting.

Section 3 defines conditional task risk and surrogate risk for pointwise scores: R(s|x)=ℓ(d∘s,P(Y|X=x)) and R_φ(s|x)=E[φ(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks δ_ℓ and δ_φ are introduced, along with global minima R* and R_φ*. Consistency is stated in two forms: (i) Fisher consistency (surrogate excess → task excess for any sequence), and (ii) a uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing ψ with ψ(ε)>0 for ε>0. A calibration function ψ(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_φ(s,x): δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε} and ̅ψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x) is defined; Corollary 3.1 says Fisher consistency is equivalent to ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x,ε, and that the biconjugate of ̅ψ yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then motivates label aggregation as necessary because using only single (X,Y) pairs is generally insufficient for Fisher consistency in the later general setting.

3.1 gives a ranking example with k items and pairwise-comparison labels Y=(i,j), meaning item i is preferred to j. A normalized transition matrix C_x is built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), with columns summing to 1; ranking is by C_x 1. A task loss ℓ(s,C) penalizes misordered scores relative to C1, and the resulting population risk R(f) is the probability that f(X) and C_X1 order differently. Proposition 1 states that for k≥3, no convex surrogate φ(·,y) is Fisher consistent for this ranking task. The section then introduces an aggregation scheme from m independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m): counts m_ij and m_j are computed, and A(Z) returns ★ if any m_j=0, otherwise a vector of normalized frequencies. Proposition 2 is about to state consistency for this aggregated setting when m≥k.

The paper now states Proposition 2: for the ranking example, define the surrogate φ(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2 for q in R^k and φ(s,⋅)=0; if m≥k, this surrogate is Fisher consistent for the ranking risk (4). The authors interpret this as evidence that aggregation enlarges the response space from Y to R^k, enabling consistency that Proposition 1 lacked.

Section 3.2 introduces aggregation more generally. For any aggregation map A:Z→A, they define the aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], pointwise excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and calibration functions ̅ψ_A(ε,x) and ̅ψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says (under an integrability bound on δ_ℓ) that φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk (2) iff ̅ψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; the Fenchel biconjugate ψ_A gives a global comparison inequality.

Section 3.2.2 shifts to a more general setting with finite label space Φ(ᵉY)=k (with a notation abuse because the ranking example previously used k for ranking length). They define an identifying surrogate φ:ℝ^d×A→ℝ via two conditions (6a)-(6b), with constants C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2}. Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. For such surrogates, the generalized majority vote aggregation A_m chooses a_y for the y minimizing empirical task loss over m labels. Corollary 3.2 states that if m=m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess implies vanishing task excess.

The section introduces level-(ξ,ζ) consistency: a comparison function ψ only needs to be linear for ε above a threshold ξ. It defines the Mammen-Tsybakov noise statistic Δ(x)=min_{incorrect s} δ_ℓ(s,x), the equivalent noise conditions (Nα) and (Mβ), and the condition number κ(x)=max_{incorrect s}δ_ℓ(s,x)/min_{incorrect s}δ_ℓ(s,x). In binary classification, Δ(x)=|2P(Y=1|X=x)-1| and κ(x)=1 when Δ(X)>0 a.s.

Theorem 1: for any (C_{φ,1},C_{φ,2})-identifying surrogate and majority-vote aggregation A_m, if 0≤ℓ≤1 and P satisfies (Nα), then whenever task excess risk exceeds a threshold 2P(κ(X)>M)+(4C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1-α)}, we get R(f)-R* ≤ (16/C_{φ,1})(aggregated surrogate excess). Hence the surrogate is level-(ξ,ζ) consistent with ζ=C_{φ,1}/16. Defining ξ_m as the infimum over M of that threshold yields ξ_m→0 as m→∞, so Corollary 3.2 follows by taking α=0.

They then derive a cruder explicit ξ_{m,k} by using κ(x)≤1/Δ(x), with separate formulas for k=2 and k≥3, and state that this yields Corollary 3.3.

Paper on robustness properties of label cleaning / aggregated labels. Abstract claims that cleaned/aggregated labels can improve robustness relative to raw-label procedures: convex surrogate minimization yields stronger task-risk consistency guarantees, and finite-dimensional classifiers can remain consistent even under loss mis-specification that breaks standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. It contrasts this with perfectly specified statistical models, where using all information is efficient, but slight loss mis-specification can destroy standard consistency. It also claims aggregation supports convergence to optimal classifiers with any fixed number of labels, and that collection, fitting, and prediction together can be robust through noisy-signal refinement.

The paper argues that label aggregation can yield consistent optimal prediction under surrogate loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including in finite-dimensional statistical settings. It contrasts the conventional supervised pipeline — collecting (X_i,Y_i), fitting a model, and ignoring cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising — with the machinery needed for modern datasets. The paper frames crowdsourced “gold standard” labels as part of this machinery and says the central issue is whether aggregation provides a necessary improvement in fitted-model consistency.

The introduction situates this work in surrogate-risk consistency theory: key results began in the 2000s, with Bartlett, Jordan, and McAuliffe characterizing convex-surrogate consistency for binary classification. Related settings include multi-label classification, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. Pair-based analyses support empirical-process theory, but do not address aggregation machinery. The paper says the main questions are whether aggregation is needed at all, whether pair-based surrogate consistency is sufficient, and in what sense aggregation improves consistency.

This part is the introduction. It argues that label aggregation is not just a practical cleaning step but can fundamentally improve consistency. Main claims: (1) in ranking, aggregation can make consistency possible where using individual labels fails; the paper points to Propositions 1–2, with failure for \(k\ge 3\) and success when enough aggregated labels are available (\(m\ge k\)). (2) In nonparametric settings, the number of aggregated labels interacts with noise conditions to improve consistency, and aggregated-label losses satisfy approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate assumptions. (3) Over restricted hypothesis classes, aggregation can restore consistency in settings where standard \((X,Y)\)-based methods fail; the intro highlights Corollary 4.1 and Theorem 2 for convergence as \(m\to\infty\). The paper frames its goal as showing both that aggregation is sometimes necessary and that it can improve robustness/consistency beyond conventional surrogate-risk theory.

Section 2 defines the learning setup and the two consistency regimes. Standard task risk is \(R(f)=E[\ell(d\circ f(X),Y)]\), with binary classification as the special case \(d(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s)\) and \(0\)-\(1\) loss. The paper then introduces a more general task risk depending on the conditional label distribution \(P(\cdot\mid X)\) and defines surrogate risk \(R_\varphi(f)=E[\varphi(f(X),Y)]\). The two settings studied are: (i) Fisher consistency with a rich hypothesis class of all Borel measurable functions, and (ii) restricted-model/statistical consistency with possibly misspecified parametric classes. The main claim here is that aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Label aggregation is formalized by replacing \(Y\) with an abstract response \(Z\) and an aggregation map \(A:Z\to\mathcal A\), leading to aggregated surrogate risk \(R_{\varphi,A}(f)=E[\varphi(f(X),A(Z))]\). Two examples are given: repeated-label aggregation, where \(Z=(Y_1,\dots,Y_m)\) with conditionally i.i.d. labels and \(A\) is empirical loss minimization/majority vote for \(0\)-\(1\) loss; and \(K\)-nearest-neighbor aggregation, where \(Z\) includes an additional i.i.d. sample and labels are aggregated over the \(K\) nearest neighbors. Appendix C is said to extend the discussion beyond this population-level setting to single-sample aggregation.

Section 3 reviews surrogate consistency in the standard rich-function-class setting. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and surrogate risk R_φ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δ_ℓ and δ_φ. Fisher consistency means asymptotic surrogate minimizers are also task-risk minimizers; the stronger uniform comparison inequality bounds task excess by surrogate excess via a nondecreasing ψ. Calibration functions are introduced: ψ(ε,x) is the pointwise minimum surrogate excess among scores with task excess at least ε, and \overlineψ(ε)=inf_x ψ(ε,x). Corollary 3.1 states Fisher consistency holds iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0, and the biconjugate of \overlineψ gives a comparison inequality.

The section then argues that single-label data can fail to admit Fisher-consistent surrogates for some tasks, motivating aggregation. The example is ranking k items from pairwise comparisons: labels are ordered pairs (i,j), an aggregated transition matrix C_x is formed from conditional pair probabilities p_ij, and ranking is based on C_x 1. The population ranking loss counts disagreements between score order and the aggregated ranking. Proposition 1 says no surrogate convex in the score argument is Fisher consistent for this ranking risk when k≥3. Finally, aggregation of m independent comparisons is introduced via counts m_ij and an aggregated response A(Z), with a special symbol ★ if some item never appears. Proposition 2 claims squared-loss regression on the aggregated response is Fisher consistent when m≥k.

Section 3.2 extends calibration theory to aggregated losses. For any aggregation method A, the conditional aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], with excess δ_{φ,A}. The pointwise and uniform calibration functions are defined in (5) as ̄ψ_A(ε,x)=inf_s{δ_{φ,A}(s,x): δ_ℓ(s,x)≥ε} and ̄ψ_A(ε)=inf_x ̄ψ_A(ε,x) (intended uniform form). Proposition 3 says that under an integrable pointwise task-risk bound b(x), φ is Fisher consistent iff ̄ψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; if ψ_A=(̄ψ_A)**, then ψ_A(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)-R_{φ,A}*. 

The section then introduces identifying surrogates. A surrogate φ is (C_{φ,1}, C_{φ,2})-identifying for finite label space Y if there exist aggregation parameters a_y and score vectors s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y such that (6a) each class y has a_y making s_y separated by margin C_{φ,1} from all scores decoding to other labels, and (6b) s_y has surrogate value within C_{φ,2} of the infimum for every other a_{y'}. This definition does not require convexity or standalone consistency. Example 3 shows binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. 

Given identifying parameters, generalized majority vote chooses A_m(y_1,...,y_m)=a_{ŷ} where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss. The text claims that for finite Y, i.i.d. samples eventually yield a random finite threshold M after which the empirical minimizer lies in the conditionally optimal label set y*(x). A corollary (Corollary 3.2) is announced: vanishing aggregated surrogate regret implies vanishing task regret as m→∞.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

Paper topic: robustness properties of label cleaning / aggregated labels. Abstract claims that using aggregated/cleaned labels can give robustness advantages over raw labels: (1) minimizing a convex surrogate loss yields stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label methods, and (2) finite-dimensional classifiers can remain consistent even under loss mis-specification, where standard uncertainty-modeling approaches fail. Introduction adds that aggregation is presented as enabling consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. It frames the paper around whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and in what sense aggregation improves consistency.

The paper sets up two regimes: unrestricted Borel function classes, where Fisher consistency is the classical notion, and parametric but potentially mis-specified classes, where aggregation is claimed to improve consistency. It defines a distribution-dependent task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(.|X))], with the zero-one loss as a special case, and also an ordinary instantaneous task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)]. Surrogate methods replace the task loss by R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)], and the paper will study consistency of such replacements.

Label aggregation is introduced via an aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))], where Z is a response replacement and A is an aggregation map. Two examples are given: repeated labeling, where Z=(Y1,…,Ym) are iid labels for the same X and A(Z) is the empirical risk minimizer over labels (majority vote for zero-one loss), and a rough K-nearest-neighbor construction, where Z includes one query point and m additional iid samples and A_{m,K} predicts by minimizing loss over the K nearest labels. The setup also notes that the repeated-sampling framework extends to aggregation from a single sample in the appendix.

steps.notes_before: The paper introduces task risk R(f) in two forms: the standard one using labels Y (eq. 1) and a conditional-distribution version depending on P(.|X) (eq. 2). It then defines surrogate risk R_\varphi(f) and says the paper studies consistency in two settings: Fisher consistency with all Borel measurable functions, and restricted parametric models that may be misspecified. Section 2.1 introduces label aggregation: replace Y by an abstract response Z, aggregate it via A: Z→A, and minimize aggregated surrogate risk R_{\varphi,A}(f)=E[\varphi(f(X),A(Z))]. Examples include repeated noisy labels with majority vote / empirical loss minimization, and K-nearest-neighbor aggregation from an input plus additional i.i.d. samples. Minor numbering issue noted: a sentence refers to “the original problem (2),” but (2) is the newer conditional-risk formulation, not the original one.

Section 3 introduces classical surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℿ contains all Borel measurable maps. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and surrogate risk R_φ(s|x), plus pointwise excess risks δ_\ell and δ_φ. Fisher consistency means surrogate excess risk → 0 implies task excess risk → 0; a stronger uniform comparison inequality uses a nondecreasing ψ with ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. Calibration functions are defined pointwise and uniformly, and Corollary 3.1 says positive calibration characterizes Fisher consistency; the Fenchel biconjugate of the uniform calibration gives the comparison function.

The section then argues that for the general task problem (2), a Fisher-consistent surrogate on individual labels would be desirable, but such results are generally impossible. Example 3.1 studies ranking from pairwise comparisons: labels are ordered pairs (i,j), a transition matrix C_x is built from conditional comparison probabilities, and ranking is based on C_x1. The resulting ranking loss is (4). Proposition 1 states that for k ≥3, any surrogate convex in the score argument is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation over m independent comparisons is then introduced via A(Z), which returns a k-vector of frequency-based quantities when every item appears and a special symbol otherwise. Proposition 2 states that squared-loss regression on this aggregated response is Fisher consistent when m ≥ k.

This part restates Proposition 2’s squared-loss result for ranking: for vectors s,q in R^k, phi(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2 and phi(s,★)=0 is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) when m≥k. It emphasizes that aggregation enlarges the response space from Y to R^k.

Section 3.2 begins. Proposition 3 extends classical calibration to aggregated risks: define aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{phi,A}(s|x), its excess delta_{phi,A}, and calibration functions overline psi_A(epsilon,x) and overline psi_A(epsilon). Under an integrable pointwise task-risk bound b(x), phi is Fisher consistent for task risk iff overline psi_A(epsilon,x)>0 for all x and epsilon>0, and the Fenchel biconjugate psi_A yields a comparison inequality psi_A(R(f)-R*) <= R_{phi,A}(f)-R_{phi,A}*.

Then Section 3.2.2 introduces identifying surrogates: a surrogate is (C_{phi,1}, C_{phi,2})-identifying if there exist aggregation parameters a_y and score vectors s_y such that (6a) separates the correct class from all decoded wrong predictions by margin C_{phi,1}, and (6b) bounds the surrogate value on incorrect aggregation parameters by C_{phi,2}. Binary hinge loss is given as an example of a (1,2)-identifying surrogate. Using identifying parameters, the paper defines generalized majority vote A_m(y1,...,ym)=a_{hat y}, where hat y minimizes empirical task loss. Because Y is finite, the sample majority vote eventually lies in the set of conditionally optimal labels y*(x), motivating Corollary 3.2 on vanishing aggregated surrogate regret as m→∞.

final_notes: Section 6 is a discussion/future work section. It argues that data cleaning vs. using all noisy labels depends on the model setting, and cites prior work supporting both sides. It identifies four future directions: (1) finite-m consistency and explicit surrogate guarantees depending on loss pair and label count, especially for ranking; (2) understanding limits imposed by the noise condition number κ(X), which can be large in multiclass settings even when the Mammen-Tsybakov noise level is low; (3) extending the mis-specified-model results beyond the current optimal-predictability assumption (Bayes-optimal classifier in F); and (4) developing restricted-hypothesis-class comparison inequalities / H-consistency analyses with label aggregation.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

Section 5 reports two numerical illustrations. For D4X/truncated quadratic loss \(\phi(\delta)=\max\{1-\delta,0\}^2\), the unaggregated H8N is \(\psi(\epsilon)=\epsilon^2\). Section 6 is discussion/future work. It contrasts unaggregated labels vs cleaning, notes finite-\(m\) consistency is unsatisfying and that ranking has explicit finite-\(m\) guarantees, and poses open problems on which problems truly require cleaning/aggregation. It also discusses fundamental limits of binary classification, mis-specified models (aggregation can succeed even when classical surrogate consistency fails), and extending comparison/aggregation ideas to restricted classes and \(\mathcal H\)-consistency.

Introduction adds that aggregation is presented as enabling consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems. The paper sets up two regimes: unrestricted Borel function classes, where Fisher consistency is the classical notion, and parametric but potentially mis-specified classes, where aggregation is claimed to improve consistency. It defines a distribution-dependent task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(.|X))], with the zero-one loss as a special case, and also an ordinary instantaneous task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)]. Surrogate methods replace the task loss by R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)], and the paper will study consistency of such replacements.

Label aggregation is introduced via an aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))], where Z is a response replacement and A is an aggregation map. Two examples are given: repeated labeling, where Z=(Y1,…,Ym) are iid labels for the same X and A(Z) is the empirical risk minimizer over labels (majority vote for zero-one loss), and a rough K-nearest-neighbor construction, where Z includes one query point and m additional iid samples and A_{m,K} predicts by minimizing loss over the K nearest labels. The setup also notes that the repeated-sampling framework extends to aggregation from a single sample in the appendix.

The section then argues that for the general task problem (2), a Fisher-consistent surrogate on individual labels would be desirable, but such results are generally impossible. Example 3.1 studies ranking from pairwise comparisons: labels are ordered pairs (i,j), a transition matrix C_x is built from conditional comparison probabilities, and ranking is based on C_x1. The resulting ranking loss is (4). Proposition 1 states that for k ≥3, any surrogate convex in the score argument is not Fisher consistent for this ranking risk. Aggregation over m independent comparisons is then introduced via A(Z), which returns a k-vector of frequency-based quantities when every item appears and a special symbol otherwise. This part restates Proposition 2’s squared-loss result for ranking: for vectors s,q in R^k, phi(s,q)=||s-q||_2^2 and phi(s,★)=0 is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) when m≥k. It emphasizes that aggregation enlarges the response space from Y to R^k.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

final_notes: Section 6 discusses implications and open problems. It argues that many consistency results depend on m→∞, whereas ranking has explicit finite-m guarantees, and calls for a theory depending jointly on (\ell,\varphi) and label count m. It says second- or third-order item comparisons (e.g., powers C_x^p from Keener) may need increasing counts. It also notes that beyond binary classification, \kappa(X) can remain large even with low N6Y noise (\alpha\approx1), while binary problems have \kappa(X)=1. For mis-specified models, the results require K7M, a Bayes-optimal classifier in \mathcal F, and show classical surrogate consistency can fail there while aggregation succeeds. It cites Nguyen et al. and Duchi et al. for joint inference of predictor and representation requiring task-loss-dependent surrogates. Finally, it suggests extending aggregation comparisons to restricted classes and unifying parametric/nonparametric advantages, with attention to how hypothesis-class size affects aggregation.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

final_notes: Section 6 is discussion/future work. It frames the paper’s message as a tradeoff between using all noisy labels and cleaning/aggregation, citing prior work on binary and multiclass settings. It emphasizes that many consistency results depend on taking m→∞, and argues that finite-m guarantees are desirable; ranking is noted as one area with explicit finite-m bounds. It highlights open problems in separating tasks that require cleaning/aggregation from those that do not, especially for higher-order comparisons. It also notes limitations of the binary-to-zero-one (B2Z) / surrogate framework: even with low noise, the complexity parameter κ(X) can be large, while binary problems have κ(X)=1. For misspecified models, the paper says the main results need a Bayes-optimal classifier in the hypothesis class, and contrasts this with prior work showing that joint inference can force task-loss-dependent surrogate forms. Finally, it suggests extending aggregation ideas to restricted hypothesis classes, potentially unifying parametric and nonparametric advantages and characterizing how class size affects aggregation.

final_notes:
Section 6 is a discussion/future-work section. It says the paper provides evidence both that un-cleaned, un-aggregated labels can have fundamental limits and that label cleaning can improve robustness. It highlights several open directions: finite-m guarantees beyond the ranking case, a surrogate consistency theory depending on both (ℓ, φ) and m, and when label aggregation is necessary.

It also summarizes the noise-condition-number viewpoint: κ(X) helps characterize comparison inequalities for multiclass problems and can remain large even when Mammen-Tsybakov noise is low (α≈1), beyond binary classification.

For misspecified models, the section states that the results in Sec. 4.3 require optimal predictability (a Bayes-optimal classifier lies in F), and suggests extending beyond this restricted setting. It references work by Nguyen et al. and Duchi et al. on jointly learning predictors and representations.

Finally, it proposes extending comparison inequalities with label aggregation to restricted hypothesis classes / H-consistency, noting that for smooth convex losses quadratic growth of ψ is rate optimal and it would be interesting to see how aggregation interacts with the size of the hypothesis class.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

Introduction motivates studying label aggregation/data cleaning as a fundamental way to improve consistency and robustness. The paper claims two main benefits: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency, where methods using aggregated labels can achieve consistent and optimal prediction in settings where this is impossible without aggregation; and (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers even when standard methods fail. It promises examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators, new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation, results on nonparametric scenarios where sample aggregation and noise conditions improve consistency, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes.

The paper introduces surrogate risk minimization for prediction with a scoring function f, decoder d, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)], and a more general risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] that depends on the conditional label distribution. It frames the main consistency settings as (i) Fisher consistency with all Borel functions in F and (ii) parametric, possibly mis-specified hypothesis classes. The central claim is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Section 2.1 defines label aggregation: instead of observing Y directly, one observes an abstract variable Z, often multiple noisy labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) for the same X. An aggregation map A:Z→A produces an aggregated label, and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. The paper asks when minimizing this aggregated surrogate risk is sufficient to minimize the task risk.

Two examples are given. In majority vote, A(Z) is the argmin over y of ∑_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is exactly majority vote. In a K-nearest-neighbor-style aggregation example, Z includes one labeled point plus m additional sample points, and A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y ∑_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_(l)) after ordering neighbors by distance. The paper says Appendix C extends the population-level discussion to aggregation from a single sample.

Section 3 formalizes surrogate consistency in the standard setting where ℓ is evaluated via a score function f and decoder d. It defines conditional task risk R(s|x) and conditional surrogate risk Rφ(s|x), along with pointwise excess risks δℓ and δφ. The paper distinguishes Fisher consistency: any sequence with surrogate risk approaching optimum must also approach optimal task risk; and a stronger uniform comparison inequality via a nondecreasing calibration function ψ. Corollary 3.1 states that Fisher consistency is characterized by positivity of the calibration function, and its Fenchel biconjugate yields a global comparison inequality.

The section then explains that in general one would like Fisher-consistent surrogates so that minimizing surrogate risk over (X,Y) pairs suffices, but such results are often impossible. As a counterexample, it considers ranking k items from pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j). The population ranking target is derived from a normalized transition matrix C_x built from p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x), and the task loss penalizes score orderings that disagree with C_x 1. The resulting population task risk is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X 1. Proposition 1 claims no convex surrogate in this setup is Fisher consistent for k≥3.

The section then foreshadows that label aggregation can restore consistency. It introduces multiple independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y1,...,Ym), defines counts m_ij and m_j, and proposes an aggregation A(Z) that maps the comparison sample to a score vector when every item appears sufficiently often; otherwise it returns a special symbol ⊥. The text states that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⊥ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

Section 3.2 extends the earlier calibration framework to aggregation. For any aggregation method A:Z→A, it defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], excess risk δ_{φ,A}, and pointwise/uniform calibration functions \barψ_A(ε,x) and \barψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 says that, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \barψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0; its Fenchel biconjugate gives a global comparison inequality ψ_A(R(f)-R*)≤R_{φ,A}(f)-R^*_{φ,A}.

The section then introduces a broad notion of an identifying surrogate. For finite label spaces (card(Y)=k), Definition 3.1 requires that for each class y there is an aggregate label a_y and parameter s_y with decoder d(s_y)=y, plus separation inequalities (6a) and (6b). Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying.

Using these identifying surrogates, the paper defines generalized majority vote aggregation A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{ŷ}, where ŷ minimizes empirical task loss over Y. As m→∞, the empirical minimizer eventually lies in the population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 states that if m(n)→∞ and φ is identifying, then vanishing aggregated surrogate excess risk implies vanishing task excess risk.

The section ends by transitioning to 3.2.3 on consistency amplification by label aggregation.

Section 4 shifts from unrestricted surrogate consistency to restricted hypothesis classes. To address this, they consider label aggregation: with m i.i.d. labels Z=(Y1,…,Ym) and majority vote A_m(Z), define ε-argmin g as {θ : g(θ) ≤ inf g + ε}. If θ_m is an ε_m-approximate minimizer of the aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A_m}(f_θ), then Corollary 4.1 says that for P optimally predictable along θ*, if ε_m→0 then R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos angle(θ_m,θ*)→1 as m→∞.

final_notes:
Section 6 discusses future work and open problems. It contrasts uncleaned vs cleaned labels: cited work by Cheng, Asi, and Duchi argues unaggregated labels can be more efficient when models capture uncertainty, while cleaning can be more robust; Dorner and Hardt favor noisy labels for validation comparisons. The paper claims its results show fundamental limits of uncleaned supervised-label information and robustness gains from cleaning.

Open problems emphasized: many consistency results rely on m→∞, which is unsatisfying; ranking has explicit finite-m guarantees, but a theory depending jointly on loss ℓ, surrogate φ, and available count m is still open. It suggests that higher-order comparisons (e.g., powers C_x^p) may require increasing counts.

It also notes limitations of binary-classification-style quantities: in broader tasks κ(X) may remain large even with low noise α≈1, while binary problems trivially have κ(X)=1. More refined task–surrogate connections, explicit failure examples, and sharper fundamental limits are suggested.

For mis-specified models, the paper says results require a Bayes-optimal classifier in F; classical surrogate consistency can fail there, though aggregation succeeds. It references prior work showing that joint inference of predictor and representation can force task-loss-dependent surrogates, motivating new approaches.

Finally, it suggests extending comparison inequalities and H-consistency results to aggregation in restricted hypothesis classes; Mao et al. are cited for rate-optimal quadratic ψ growth for smooth convex loss, and an aggregation-based extension is proposed to unify parametric and nonparametric advantages.

Paper title: "Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning" by Chen Cheng and John Duchi. Abstract claims that learning procedures using aggregated labels / label information distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties unavailable without data cleaning. It says these procedures yield stronger risk-consistency guarantees than those possible with raw labels, and that while standard approaches may fail when the loss is even slightly mis-specified, procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers.

The paper studies how aggregating/cleaning labels affects surrogate risk consistency. It asks whether aggregation is necessary and how it helps, arguing that it can provide robustness and consistency not achievable with raw (X,Y) pairs alone. The introduction claims concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where methods using only pairs (X,Y) fail but label aggregation yields consistency. It also says the paper develops new theory for surrogate consistency with aggregated labels, including in fully nonparametric settings where the number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency, and in restricted hypothesis classes where aggregation can guarantee consistency. It mentions that losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities, with a multiclass threshold O(m^{-1}) at α=1/2.

The paper sets up standard supervised learning with inputs X, labels Y, scoring functions f:X->R^d, decoder d:R^d->Y, task risk R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),Y)] in (1), and a distribution-dependent version R(f)=E[ℓ(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] in (2). It then studies surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)] and says consistency is considered in two settings: (i) Fisher consistency with F all Borel functions, and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. The main message is that label aggregation improves consistency in both settings.

Label aggregation: instead of Y, one observes Z in an abstract space 𝒵; in repeated labeling, Z=(Y1,…,Ym) with Yi|X=x iid~P(Y|X=x). An aggregation map A:𝒵->𝒜 produces A(Z), and the aggregated surrogate risk is R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] in (3).

Example 1: majority vote. A(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ℓ(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote.

Example 2: K-nearest-neighbor aggregation. Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m) with an additional iid sample, order neighbors by distance to X, and define A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ℓ(y,Y_{(l)}). The paper says Appendix C extends beyond this population-level setup to aggregation from a single sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n.

The paper defines conditional task and surrogate risks in Section 3, plus pointwise excess risks and minimal risks R* and R_φ*. It distinguishes Fisher consistency and a stronger uniform comparison inequality with calibration functions; Corollary 3.1 states Fisher consistency iff ψ(ε,x)>0 for all x, and a positive calibrated ψ yields ψ(R(f)-R*) ≤ R_φ(f)-R_φ*. The text argues that for ordinary risk minimization with only single pairs (X,Y), consistent surrogate minimization is generally impossible, motivating label aggregation.

Section 3.1 gives a ranking example with pairwise comparison labels Y=(i,j) over k items. It defines a normalized transition matrix C_x from pairwise probabilities p_ij and uses C_x 1 to induce a ranking; task risk R(f) is the probability that f(X) orders items differently from C_X1. Proposition 1 says no convex surrogate φ is Fisher consistent for this ranking problem when k≥3.

The section then introduces aggregation for multiple independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m): counts m_ij and m_j are used to define an aggregation A(Z), returning ⋆ if some item never appears and otherwise a vector of normalized counts. The text claims that regressing on A(Z) when A(Z)≠⋆ yields consistency, with Proposition 2 to follow.

The paper introduces a general aggregation-aware surrogate framework. For any aggregation A:Z→A, it defines the conditional surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(s|x)=E[φ(s,A(Z))|X=x], the pointwise excess risk δ_{φ,A}(s,x), and corresponding calibration functions \overlineψ_A(ε,x) and \overlineψ_A(ε). Proposition 3 extends the earlier calibration result: under an integrable excess-loss bound, φ is Fisher consistent for the task risk iff \overlineψ_A(ε,x)>0 for all x and ε>0, and a biconjugate calibration function yields a comparison inequality between task excess risk and surrogate excess risk.

The paper then shifts to consistency amplification via label aggregation. It assumes finite label space \mathcal{Y} and defines an identifying surrogate (Def. 3.1): for each class y there are surrogate parameters a_y and points s_y such that s_y decodes to y and the loss at (s_y,a_y) is separated by margins from losses for incorrect decodings and from the global infimum for other labels. Example 3 shows the binary hinge loss is (1,2)-identifying. Using such a surrogate, it defines a generalized majority-vote aggregator A_m(y_1,…,y_m)=a_{\hat y}, where \hat y minimizes empirical task loss over labels. Corollary 3.2 states that if m→∞ and the surrogate is identifying, surrogate consistency of f_n under aggregated labels implies consistency for the original task risk.

Section 6 is a discussion/future-work section. It frames the paper’s contributions as showing limitations of using uncleaned supervised labels and benefits of cleaning. It highlights open problems around finite m guarantees, noting that many consistency results rely on m→∞ and that a joint theory depending on the loss/surrogate pair and count m remains open. It says ranking has explicit finite-m guarantees, but extending such guarantees to other settings (including higher-order item comparisons like powers C_x^p) is an open direction.

It also discusses limits of binary-to-zero-one (B2Z) results: even with low noise and α≈1, κ(X) may remain large, while binary problems trivially have κ(X)=1. It argues that stronger task–surrogate connections and sharper failure constructions are needed.

For mis-specified models, it says the results require K7M, a Bayes-optimal classifier in F; classical surrogate consistency can fail there while aggregation succeeds. It references Nguyen et al. and Duchi et al. as showing that joint inference of predictor and representation can force task-loss-dependent surrogate forms.

Finally, it suggests extending aggregation comparisons to restricted classes, citing H-consistency work and Mao et al.’s quadratic ψ growth for smooth convex loss, with an interest in unifying parametric and nonparametric advantages and understanding how hypothesis-class size affects aggregation.

Section 4 begins a new theme: robustness/consistency for restricted hypothesis classes. It argues aggregation can restore consistency when optimization is limited to a class ℒ instead of all measurable functions. 

4.1 Binary classification: λ(y,d(s))? Actually binary 0-1 loss with margin surrogate φ(s,y)=φ(sy). Over all measurable functions, classical Fisher/uniform consistency holds iff φ'(0)<0. But in a linear class f_θ(x)=<θ,x>, even if the distribution is optimally predictable by some θ*, Proposition 4 says there are distributions where every surrogate minimizer has worse target risk than θ* and can be nearly orthogonal to θ* (cosine ≤ ε for any ε>0). 

Aggregation is then introduced via majority vote A_m on m i.i.d. samples and ε-argmin sets. Corollary 4.1: if the optimization tolerance ε_m→0, then aggregated minimizers satisfy R(f_{θ_m})→R(f_{θ*}) and cos angle(θ_m,θ*)→1.

4.2 Multiclass setting: Ψ={1,...,k}, zero-one loss, decoder argmax. The surrogate φ(s,y) is assumed Fisher consistent and to satisfy a limiting-loss condition φ(s,y)→0 when the correct score dominates all others (φ goes to 0 under infinite margins). Examples: multiclass logistic loss and sum-of-pairwise convex nonincreasing losses with φ'(0)<0 and inf φ=0. The section notes Zhang's consistency result for the zero-sum linear class {f:1^Tf=0}. The binary case fits this framework by taking scores (g(x),-g(x)) with measurable g.

steps.notes_before: Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main contribution is VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework for auditing social representation/bias in video generation, focused on gender and ethnicity. It contrasts aligned video diffusion models with unaligned likelihood-trained baselines and argues alignment tuning can amplify bias. The framework uses deterministic prompts built from event templates of the form ⟨p,a,c⟩: actor p, verb a, context c. It uses 42 curated verbs and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino). The paper also states the controlled gender space includes four categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person. Table 1 gives prompt counts: 42 person-only prompts and 294 ethnicity+person prompts. In the prompt design section, the paper says all prompts are fixed, non-LLM-generated, and demographic attributes are analyzed post hoc from generated videos. In the evaluation section, it uses three VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B), samples 16 frames per video, and aggregates frame/video predictions by majority vote and ensemble.

The paper next introduces Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS), a video-level temporal metric: for each video, TAS is the percentage of frames whose classified attribute matches the final majority-voted label for that video. High TAS means stable temporal identity portrayal; low TAS indicates flickering/inconsistency.

It then defines an ethnicity-aware gender fairness metric, Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG), computed for each verb and ethnicity group in the ethnicity+gender setting. PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total, with values in [-1,1]. A PBSG of 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male-to-female ratio, and -0.5 to the inverse. Positive values indicate male bias, negative values female bias, and 0 is used as a diagnostic parity target rather than a real-world ground truth. The paper says this metric captures how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group and whether bias is amplified for specific ethnicities.

A footnote/aside says standalone gender-only analysis is not used because without explicit ethnicity specifications the model mostly generates White individuals, so gender-only results would effectively be White-only.

The paper defines Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) as a video-level temporal metric: for each video, it is the percentage of frames whose classified attribute matches the final majority-voted label for that video. Higher TAS means more stable identity portrayal; lower TAS means more flicker/inconsistency.

It also defines an ethnicity-aware gender fairness metric, Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG), used for each verb and ethnicity group in the ethnicity+gender setting: PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total, with values in [-1,1]. PBSG = 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male-to-female ratio, and -0.5 to the inverse. Positive values indicate male bias, negative values female bias, and 0 is used as a diagnostic parity target. The metric is meant to capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group and whether bias is amplified for specific ethnicities. A footnote says standalone gender-only analysis is not used because without explicit ethnicity specifications the model mostly generates White individuals, so gender-only results would be effectively White-only.

For ethnicity bias, the paper uses two metrics: Representation Deviation Score for Ethnicity (RDS_e) and Simpson’s Diversity Index (SDI). For each ethnic group e, P_e = N_e/N_total, where N_e is the number of outputs identified as ethnicity e. RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|, and with seven ethnic groups the ideal balanced probability is 1/7 ≈ 14.3%. Positive RDS_e means overrepresentation; negative means underrepresentation. SDI = 1 - sum_e P_e^2, with higher values indicating more diverse/balanced distributions. The paper says the uniform baseline is a diagnostic benchmark, not a real-world demographic target.

For bias shift between unaligned and aligned models, the paper computes ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI to measure directional change; shifts toward more balanced gender ratios, reduced ethnic skew, or higher diversity are interpreted as improvement.
