The paper then frames its main research question around how alignment tuning shapes social-attribute distributions and outlines sections on reward-dataset demographics, reward-model bias, and the effect of biased reward models on video outputs.

Section 5 studies social bias in image reward datasets and reward models. It analyzes HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic by extracting gender/ethnicity/verb from captions with GPT-4o-mini and from images with three VLMs, keeping only predefined verbs. HPDv2 has 28,783 validated tuples over 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples over 19 verbs. Gender preference analysis on valid man–woman pairs finds HPDv2 leans male: 26 verbs qualify, and 69.23% (18/26) prefer men. Pick-a-Pic leans female: 18 verbs qualify, and 61.11% (11/18) prefer women. Ethnicity preference in both datasets favors White strongly (43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic), then East Asian and Indian; some verbs show other specific preferences (e.g., bake→Black, fish→East Asian). The section then introduces a benchmark for reward-model bias using FLUX-generated images with two settings: Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, 100 images per prompt, summarized in Table 3 and Figure 5.

Section 5 continues with the benchmark for image reward models. Table 3 reports prompt counts for two benchmark settings: Ethnicity + Person (294 prompts) and Ethnicity + Gender (1176 prompts). The example prompts are “An East Asian person is baking cookies...” and “An East Asian woman is baking cookies...”. The authors argue FLUX is used only as a controlled generator, not assumed bias-free. A human verification study on 100 randomly sampled images found 77% unanimous agreement and 97% majority agreement (only 3 images lacked consensus), suggesting low label noise.

Figure 5 shows example images for prompts of the form “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context],” but only for man/woman gendered cases.

Preference Bias Evaluation: four reward models are tested—HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, and CLIP as the shared base model. Each image gets a continuous scalar preference score. Table 4 summarizes bias metrics averaged across 42 verbs: ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation distribution (RDS, with overall SDI). CLIP has near-neutral or slightly negative PBSG overall (-0.0726) and SDI 0.8495. HPSv2.0 shows strong positive overall PBSG (0.6039) and slightly lower SDI (0.8492), while HPSv2.1 and PickScore have slightly negative overall PBSG (-0.0984 and -0.1157) and SDIs of 0.8470 and 0.8483, respectively.

Section 5’s bias evaluation uses two prompt schemes. For ethnicity-aware gender bias, evaluation prompts omit gender (“A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]”), while generation prompts specify ethnicity and gender (“A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is ...”). Scores are standardized, averaged over 100 images per generation prompt, then PBSG is computed by subtracting women’s average from men’s for each ethnicity/verb. Positive PBSG means men-preference; negative means women-preference. Reported overall PBSG values are CLIP –0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 –0.0984, and PickScore –0.1157. The text says HPSv2.0’s strong man-preference is consistent across ethnic groups, while the others show woman-preference biases.

For ethnicity bias, evaluation prompts omit ethnicity (“A person is [verb]-ing [context]”), while generation prompts specify ethnicity (“A/An [ethnicity] person is ...”). Scores are standardized and averaged over 100 images per generation prompt. RDS and SDI are computed by fixing the verb and applying softmax across ethnicities. Positive RDS indicates overrepresentation; higher SDI indicates more balanced outputs. CLIP slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182) and has the highest SDI (0.8495). After fine-tuning, HPSv2.0 shifts toward Middle Eastern (RDS = 0.0315), HPSv2.1 toward Latino (RDS = 0.0382), and PickScore toward East Asian (RDS = 0.0352), with all showing reduced SDI.

Section 6 studies social bias after preference alignment in video generation. They fine-tune a VCM distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore via single-step latent consistency distillation and evaluate with the same framework as Section 4. Table 5 reports PBSG (gender bias across ethnic groups), RDSe (ethnicity representation disparity), and SDI (overall diversity), averaged over 42 verbs. For the base VCM-VC2, PBSG is high and positive across ethnicities (overall 0.8034), indicating strong man bias; White is overrepresented (RDS 0.6405) while Black, East Asian, and Middle Eastern are underrepresented, with SDI 0.1433. HPSv2.0 increases man bias further (overall PBSG 0.9116) and lowers SDI to 0.1257. HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce PBSG substantially (overall 0.2267 and 0.3714) and have lower SDI than the base, with PickScore giving the highest SDI among the aligned models (0.1467). Missing ethnicity values in Table 5 indicate zero recognizable instances under the person-only condition. Table 6 reports Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) for ethnicity and gender; higher TAS means more stable identity across video frames, and all three aligned models improve TAS over the base model for both attributes.

Table 6 shows temporal identity stability improves with alignment. For ethnicity, mean TAS rises from 0.8904 (VCM-VC2 baseline) to 0.9632 after HPSv2.1, and perfect-stability videos increase from 0.5670 to 0.8330 (+0.2660). For gender, stability reaches 0.9895 with 0.9440 perfect stability. TAS standard deviation also drops (e.g., by 0.0654 for ethnicity), indicating more uniform frame-level consistency. However, improved stability can also entrench bias: HPSv2.0 increases overall PBSG from 0.8034 to 0.9116 and yields very stable biased gender outputs (TAS 0.9967; 0.9830 perfect stability). The section concludes that alignment can either mitigate or amplify bias depending on the reward model; HPSv2.0 reinforces male/White preference, whereas HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce man-dominant bias but still leave residual ethnic disparities. The paper argues that social bias in aligned video diffusion models is largely inherited from the reward model’s bias profile.

It also warns that preference data can be used both for bias mitigation and for exclusionary or propagandistic manipulation. The supplementary inventory lists items A, C, D, F, G and several numbered plots/analyses covering gender and ethnicity, including 42-verb analyses, WebVid-10M training-data effects, reward-model and aligned-video analyses, and controllable-preference analyses. The acknowledgment thanks reviewers and lists funding/support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving’s Technical AI Safety Research Program, with the standard disclaimer that the authors’ views do not represent those organizations.

Key metrics: L2V (PBSG) = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total in [-1,1], where positive values favor men and negative values favor women; gender-only analysis is excluded because absent specified ethnicity the model predominantly depicts White individuals. Shift metrics are ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, and ΔW3H, with more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, or higher diversity treated as improvement.

Claimed contributions: (1) a comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit of bias in aligned video diffusion; (2) the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance and amplification of bias; and (3) evidence that alignment can simultaneously improve visual quality/coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing social composition, plus guidance via controlled/counter-biased preference data for mitigation.

Section 7 presents controllable gender preference modeling for video diffusion. Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation, rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Limitations: the gender/ethnicity categories are practical but socially constructed, missing fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; future work should include richer intersectional groups. Human-validated VLM judges are still image-level classifiers and can be biased/inaccurate, especially on stylized or ambiguous frames; ensembling helps but does not solve this. The alignment experiments mainly use single-step latent consistency distillation with limited rewards, so RL-based tuning and multi-turn video instruction alignment may behave differently. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation only shows targeted modulation and does not address broader value alignment or long-term societal impact. The fixed socially associated action taxonomy limits generalization to open-ended generation and novel actions.

Section 8’s broader impact says alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, so developers should monitor generated social composition with audits like QX2 rather than relying on aesthetic/preference metrics alone. final_notes: Broader Impact Statement: the paper argues that alignment in video generation can unintentionally stabilize and entrench bias, making stereotypes appear natural and authoritative when artifacts/flicker are removed. It also notes dual-use risks: the same preference-data machinery can be used for bias mitigation or for exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda. Developers are urged to monitor generated social composition continuously with multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2, and to curate preference data with rigor so it reflects a diverse, equitable society. The supplementary inventory lists items A, C, D, F, and G plus multiple numbered gender/ethnicity plots and analyses covering 42 verbs/actions, reward-model and reward-aligned video analyses, ethnicity preferences, and training/inference details.

Developers are urged to monitor generated social composition continuously with multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2, and to curate preference data with rigor so it reflects a diverse, equitable society. final_notes: Section 8 concludes that VideoBiasEval fills blind spots in text-to-video social-bias evaluation by separating identity attributes from content semantics and tracking how alignment changes representation. It argues reward-based alignment can inherit and amplify biases in human preference data, so bias auditing and mitigation are needed throughout generation. The limitations section adds that the study uses predefined gender/ethnicity categories, image-level VLM evaluators, a single-step latent consistency distillation setup with limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference manipulations, and a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions, which may constrain generalization. Broader impact emphasizes that alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, and that controllable preference modeling is dual-use: the same method can mitigate or intensify representational harm. It recommends continuous auditing with multi-granular event-centric frameworks such as VideoBiasEval and careful, equitable preference-data curation.

Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. Section 7 studies controllable gender bias in video diffusion models by composing gender-skewed preference data. Two reward datasets are built from the Ethnicity+Gender set: a man-preferred version and a woman-preferred version, each with 2.94 million same-action/same-ethnicity preference pairs, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs for diversity. Ethnicity bias is evaluated with two metrics. Representation Deviation Score for Ethnicity (RDS_e) is defined as P_e - 1/|E|, where P_e = N_e/N_total over identifiable outputs and E is the set of ethnic groups. With seven groups, the uniform benchmark is 1/7 (~14.3%); positive RDS_e means overrepresentation and negative means underrepresentation. Example: RDS_e = 0.769 corresponds to about 91.2% representation for one group. The paper stresses that this uniform baseline is only a diagnostic benchmark for the neutral person-only setting, not a claim about real-world demographics. Simpson’s Diversity Index (SDI) is 1 - sum_e P_e^2; higher SDI means more diverse/balanced representation, lower SDI means concentration in a few groups. The paper also defines bias shift between unaligned and aligned models using ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; improvement means more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, and higher diversity. final_notes: Section 7 studies controllable gender bias in video diffusion using deliberately composed preference data. It constructs two image reward datasets from the Ethnicity+Gender set: a man-preferred and a woman-preferred version, each with 2.94 million same-action, same-ethnicity pairs; male images are labeled 1 in the man-preferred set and 0 in the woman-preferred set, with labels reversed for the woman-preferred set. An additional 537,660 HPDv2 image pairs are added for face-free diversity. Two reward models are fine-tuned on CLIP: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 shows RMM scores much higher than CLIP across all groups, while RMW scores are lower, indicating opposite directional preferences. Table 8 shows RMM raises PBSG from 0.8034 to 0.9584, while RMW lowers it to 0.3082, suggesting counter-biased alignment can reduce male preference and move toward more balanced portrayals. The section also analyzes 42 actions and reports that sleep, stretch, and read are the most sensitive under both preference directions. Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation are needed throughout the generation pipeline; it summarizes that preference data and reward models show directional biases, alignment can amplify inherited bias (Table 5: VCM-VC2 0.8034 to +HPSv2.0 0.9116), and reward design can counter bias (Table 8: VCM-VC2 0.8034 to +RMW 0.3082). The Limitations section says the study uses predefined U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity categories, human-validated VLM evaluators with image-level classification, single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models, synthetic gender-preference manipulations, and a fixed set of 42 actions. The Broader Impact section argues alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, preference control is dual-use, and developers should continuously audit social composition and curate preferences responsibly. The Acknowledgment lists support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, and the Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving, and disclaims endorsement by those organizations.

VideoBiasEval is a video bias evaluation framework that uses event-based prompts and multi-granular metrics to assess ethnicity and gender bias. It separates semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes and uses VLMs to infer gender/ethnicity across frames and aggregate annotations. The abstract claims the paper is the first end-to-end analysis linking human preference biases in datasets, their amplification in reward models, and their propagation into aligned video diffusion models. Alignment is said to strengthen representational biases and make them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped videos.

Quantitative claims noted so far: in Section 5.1, 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs show man preference, while 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs show woman preference. VideoBiasEval evaluates bias by varying actor gender and ethnicity across 42 socially associated verbs in real-world event prompts, then extracting attributes from generated videos. An event is a tuple <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. The verb list is: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. Two conditions are defined: Person-only (42 prompts, one per verb) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities). Table 1 gives prompt counts/examples. The paper says Ethnicity+Person already isolates ethnicity effects, so no separate ethnicity-only condition is used.

Section 3.3 defines multi-granular evaluation using three VLM judges: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B. They uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Each judge assigns binary gender labels (man/woman) and one of seven ethnicity labels (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino). The pipeline uses majority voting within each model to produce video-level labels, then fuses labels across models.

TAS (Temporal Attribute Stability) is the fraction of frames whose label matches the final majority-voted label; low TAS indicates attribute flickering. Bias metrics include PBSG = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total, interpreted as male/female skew, with 0 as balance. The paper frames PBSG as ethnicity-aware gender bias within each verb/ethnicity group. It also defines ethnicity bias with RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E| and SDI = 1 - sum_e P_e^2, where |E| = 7. RDS measures over/underrepresentation relative to uniform 1/7, and SDI measures overall diversity. Finally, bias shift metrics ΔPBSG, ΔRDSe, and ΔSDI compare aligned vs. baseline models; improvement means more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, or greater diversity.

Section 4 evaluates four video diffusion models in two aligned–unaligned pairs: ModelScope vs InstructVideo, and VideoCrafter-2 vs T2V-Turbo-V1. Each prompt generates 10 videos, results averaged over 42 verbs. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG), ethnicity representation (RDS_e), and overall diversity (SDI) for ethnicity+person prompts and person-only prompts.

Table 2 values: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, InstructVideo 0.5295 (Δ +0.0480); VideoCrafter-2 0.7581, T2V-Turbo-V1 0.8306 (Δ +0.0725). Thus alignment increases male imbalance overall. Across all ethnic groups, mean PBSG is positive. For person-only prompts, White RDS is highest in both baseline models: ModelScope 0.7690, InstructVideo 0.7833, VideoCrafter-2 0.6905, T2V-Turbo-V1 0.6381. SDI values: 0.0538, 0.0267, 0.1252, 0.1119 respectively. The text concludes alignment can worsen gender disparity while sometimes reducing White dominance, but may also lower overall diversity.

Table note: positive PBSG means man-preference, negative means woman-preference; positive RDS_e means overrepresentation. Missing RDS entries (—) indicate zero recognizable instances for that ethnicity under person-only prompts.

Section 4 includes human evaluation of 400 generated videos by three independent annotators experienced in social-bias analysis. They use standardized guidelines and judge whether prompted attributes are reflected, not subjective/normative aspects. The three-VLM majority-vote ensemble correlates with human judgments at Pearson 0.89 for gender and 0.73 for ethnicity. Agreement is also high: Cohen’s Kappa is 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ Kappa is 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. A high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions has consensus rates of 99.0% for gender and 83.3% for ethnicity; PBSG changes only from 0.846 to 0.863 (p=0.68) and SDI from 0.745 to 0.761, so the paper treats the metrics as stable under this restriction. The section argues the evaluator is reliable and human-aligned, and transitions to Section 5 on image reward datasets and trained rewards.

Section 5 begins the analysis of social biases in image reward datasets and reward models. It examines HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic, using GPT-4o-mini to extract gender, ethnicity, and verbs from captions and VLMs to classify image attributes, retaining validated tuples with a predefined verb. After processing, HPDv2 has 28,783 tuples covering 29 verbs and Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs. For gender, the paper analyzes pairs where preferred and dispreferred images differ in gender: HPDv2 has 26/42 qualifying verbs and is mostly man-preferred (69.23%, 18/26), while Pick-a-Pic has 18/42 qualifying verbs and is mostly woman-preferred (61.11%, 11/18). For ethnicity, White representations are most preferred overall in both datasets (43.34% in HPDv2, 40.08% in Pick-a-Pic), followed by East Asian and Indian representations, with some verb-specific deviations like “bake” favoring Black individuals and “fish” favoring East Asians. The section argues these preferences may transmit bias into reward training.

Section 5.2 then constructs a controlled text-to-image benchmark to study reward-model preferences. Using FLUX and event templates from Section 3.2, it creates prompts varying gender, ethnicity, and verb in two settings: Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender. Table 3 reports 294 prompts for Ethnicity+Person and 1176 for Ethnicity+Gender, with 100 images generated per prompt. The goal is to isolate reward-model preferences independently of generator-specific artifacts.

final_notes: Section 8/Limitations: The paper says its evaluation covers two social dimensions—gender and ethnicity—using predefined U.S. Census/prior-literature categories, which the authors note are socially constructed and limited for intersectional/cultural nuance. The VLM-based evaluators rely on image-level classification and may have biases, though an ensemble is used; more human annotations would help. The study mainly tests a specific alignment method (single-step latent consistency distillation) and a limited set of reward models, so other protocols (RL-based tuning, multi-turn instruction alignment) may differ. The controllable preference modeling experiments only manipulate gender preference synthetically. VideoBiasEval is benchmarked on 42 socially associated actions, which may limit generalization to open-ended or novel actions. Broader impact statement: The authors argue alignment tuning can act as a "bias stabilizer," making stereotyped representations more polished and harder to detect, and they describe controllable preference modeling as dual-use because curated preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes. They recommend moving beyond aesthetic metrics to multi-granular, event-centric auditing such as VideoBiasEval and treating preference-data curation as seriously as model design. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Authors listed; equal contribution and equal advising noted. Abstract claims the paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation in video generation. It uses event-based prompting to separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). It defines multi-granular metrics for (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. The paper claims an end-to-end analysis from human preference datasets to reward models and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, finding that alignment tuning amplifies representational biases and makes them temporally stable, leading to smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 reiterates the framework and says VLMs infer gender/ethnicity across frames and aggregate them for bias quantification.

Introduction defines “aligned models” as video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, contrasted with unaligned likelihood-only baselines. Alignment is described as reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. The paper argues that preference data may encode social biases that downstream aligned generators inherit, motivating the question of how alignment changes social-attribute distributions in video models. It claims prior evaluation frameworks are insufficient because they use non-diverse prompts, lack comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and do not track before-vs-after alignment shifts. VideoBiasEval is introduced as an event-based prompting framework that separates verb/semantic content from actor identity attributes, enabling controlled assessment across contexts. The paper focuses on gender and ethnicity. It proposes multi-granular metrics for (1) ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distribution shifts across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos.

The paper first examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic, then checks whether image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) inherit those preferences, and finally fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 with these reward models to study before-vs-after alignment. The reported findings are that both preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and strong White favoritism; reward models inherit and amplify these biases; and alignment tuning shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) suggests alignment improves temporal consistency but can make biased portrayals more persistent. The paper also says it studies whether curated reward datasets can intentionally control bias representation, analyzes preference shifts across 42 events, and offers guidance via targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling. Contributions claimed: VideoBiasEval, an end-to-end pipeline from preference datasets to reward models to aligned video generators, and evidence that preference alignment improves quality/coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing social composition.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework for measuring social bias in video generation. It defines each event as a tuple ⟨p,a,c⟩: actor p, verb a, context c. The framework uses structured prompts that vary gender and ethnicity across real-world events, then generates videos with diffusion models and evaluates social-attribute consistency/fairness from the outputs. The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 socially associated verbs (e.g., bake, bike, clean, cook, drive, read, run, walk). The section emphasizes that this bounded setup is meant to support reproducible, interpretable bias analysis and the first end-to-end tracing of bias propagation in video generation.

It then discusses video-level fairness metrics, starting with Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias using the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG), defined as (N_man - N_woman)/N_total in [-1,1]. A positive value indicates male bias, negative female bias, and 0 is used as a parity benchmark for controlled bias auditing rather than a real-world distribution claim. The text says gender-only analysis is not emphasized because without explicit ethnicity prompts the model mostly generates White individuals, so gender-only results would effectively reflect White demographic bias. The paper frames PBSG as measuring gender balance within each ethnic group and stereotype amplification across ethnicity-conditioned verbs.

The paper now adds ethnicity bias metrics. It defines Representation Deviation Score for Ethnicity (RDS_e) as P_e - 1/|E|, where P_e = N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnic outputs. With seven groups, the uniform benchmark is 1/7 (~14.3%), and positive/negative RDS_e indicates over-/underrepresentation. It emphasizes this is a parity baseline for controlled bias auditing, not a claim about real-world demographics. The paper also defines Simpson’s Diversity Index (SDI) = 1 - sum_e P_e^2, where higher SDI means more diverse/balanced representation. Finally, it says bias shift is analyzed between unaligned and aligned models using ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; movement toward more balanced gender ratios, reduced ethnic skew, or higher diversity is interpreted as improvement.

PBSG is computed from evaluation prompts of the form “A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]” and generation prompts of the form “A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context]”; reward scores are standardized, averaged over 100 images per generation prompt, then men’s average minus women’s average is taken for each ethnicity-verb pair. For ethnicity bias, evaluation prompts omit ethnicity (“A person is [verb]-ing [context]”), while generation prompts specify ethnicity (“A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]”). Scores are standardized and softmaxed over ethnicities per verb to compute RDSe and SDI. CLIP slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182) and has the highest SDI (0.8495); after fine-tuning, HPSv2.0 shifts toward Middle Eastern, HPSv2.1 toward Latino, and PickScore toward East Asian individuals, with all showing reduced SDI.

Male images are labeled 1 in the man-preferred set and 0 in the woman-preferred set, with the opposite labeling for the woman-preferred set.

Table 7 reports that RMM has positive preference bias scores across all demographic groups (average 1.5280, White 1.6300, Black 1.5752, Latino 1.5524, East Asian 1.4323, Southeast Asian 1.4525, India 1.5619, Middle Eastern 1.4914), while RMW has negative scores across all groups (average -0.7448, with group scores around -0.63 to -0.88). It claims alignment with RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in actions like exercise, row, and cook, while RMW shifts portrayals toward women-preferred actions like bake, sleep, and sweep. The section concludes that even semantically neutral activities can show large gender shifts under alignment and argues for event-level auditing and careful, community-informed use of controllable preference modeling.

Section 8 concludes that VideoBiasEval exposes blind spots in evaluating social bias in text-to-video generation. It claims the framework decouples identity attributes from content semantics and tracks how alignment tuning reshapes social representations. The authors conclude that reward-model-based alignment can inherit and often amplify biases encoded in human preference data, and they call for bias auditing and mitigation throughout the video generation pipeline to support more equitable generative systems.

Section 8/Limitations: The paper says its evaluation covers two social dimensions—gender and ethnicity—using predefined U.S. Census/prior-literature categories, which the authors note are socially constructed and limited for intersectional/cultural nuance. The VLM-based evaluators rely on image-level classification and may have biases, though an ensemble is used; more human annotations would help. The study mainly tests a specific alignment method (single-step latent consistency distillation) and a limited set of reward models, so other protocols (RL-based tuning, multi-turn instruction alignment) may differ. The controllable preference modeling experiments only manipulate gender preference synthetically. VideoBiasEval is benchmarked on 42 socially associated actions, which may limit generalization to open-ended or novel actions.

Broader impact statement: The authors argue alignment tuning can act as a “bias stabilizer,” making stereotyped representations more polished and harder to detect, and they describe controllable preference modeling as dual-use because curated preference datasets can amplify or suppress social attributes. They recommend moving beyond aesthetic metrics to multi-granular, event-centric auditing such as VideoBiasEval and treating preference-data curation as seriously as model design.

final_notes: Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation, rather than relying on preference alignment alone. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories (from U.S. Census conventions and prior literature) are socially constructed and miss fluidity, intersectionality, and cultural nuance; richer intersectional groups are future work. Human-validated VLM judges are still image-level classifiers and can be biased/inaccurate, especially for stylized or ambiguous frames; ensembling helps but does not remove this. Alignment experiments rely mainly on single-step latent consistency distillation with limited rewards, so RL-based tuning and multi-turn instruction alignment may behave differently. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation only shows targeted modulation and does not solve broader value alignment, normative appropriateness, or long-term societal impact. The fixed action taxonomy also limits generalization to open-ended or novel actions. Broader impact section argues alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, supports dual-use concerns, and says aesthetic metrics are insufficient; developers should monitor generated social composition with multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2. The supplement inventory lists items A, C, D, F, G and multiple numbered gender/ethnicity plots, including dataset ethnicity item 10 and ethnicity plot 38.

Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation, rather than relying on preference alignment alone. Limitations: the paper notes that predefined gender/ethnicity categories (from U.S. Census conventions and prior literature) are socially constructed and miss fluidity, intersectionality, and cultural nuance; richer intersectional groups are future work. Human-validated VLM judges are still image-level classifiers and can be biased/inaccurate, especially for stylized or ambiguous frames; ensembling helps but does not remove this. Alignment experiments rely mainly on single-step latent consistency distillation with limited rewards, so RL-based tuning and multi-turn instruction alignment may behave differently. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation only shows targeted modulation and does not solve broader value alignment, normative appropriateness, or long-term societal impact. The fixed action taxonomy also limits generalization to open-ended or novel actions.

final_notes: Section 10 (Broader Impact) argues that as video diffusion models scale, alignment can both improve quality and stabilize bias: removing artifacts and flicker can make stereotypes look more natural and authoritative. It says controllable preference modeling is dual-use: the same method can mitigate or intensify representational harm, because curated reward data can amplify or suppress attributes, with possible risks including exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda. The section recommends continuous auditing of social composition using multi-granular event-centric frameworks such as VideoBiasEval and treats preference-data curation as requiring the same rigor as architecture design. It cites results from Tables 5–8 as evidence that alignment can increase PBSG/TAS and that different preference datasets steer social portrayals in opposite directions. The acknowledgment adds funding sources: AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, and Technical AI Safety Research Program funding at Coefficient Giving. No new empirical evidence is provided for the broader societal-risk claims beyond these cited tables.

steps.notes_before: Section 3.3 introduces multi-granular event-centric bias evaluation using three open-source VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B). They uniformly sample 16 frames per video and first majority-vote frame labels to get video-level labels, then fuse across models. Frame/video analysis covers temporal attribute stability (TAS), gender bias, ethnicity bias, and bias shifts between aligned and unaligned models. Here, gender bias is operationalized only with binary labels man/woman via PBSG, while ethnicity uses seven groups and metrics RDS_e and SDI. A footnote says gender-only analysis is omitted because without explicit ethnicity specifications models mostly produce White individuals, so gender-alone analysis would mainly reflect White demographic bias.

Section 4 evaluates four video diffusion models in two aligned–unaligned pairs: ModelScope vs InstructVideo, and VideoCrafter-2 vs T2V-Turbo-V1. For each prompt, each model generates 10 videos with different seeds; results are averaged over 42 verbs. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI). Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. It analyzes two human preference datasets: HPDv2 (28,783 validated image-caption-preference tuples, 29 verbs) and Pick-a-Pic (14,958 tuples, 19 verbs). Gender preference analysis filters to valid man–woman pairs: 26/42 verbs in HPDv2 qualify, with 69.23% (18/26) preferring men; 18/42 verbs in Pick-a-Pic qualify, with 51.11% (11/18) preferring women. Ethnicity preference analysis shows both datasets favor White representations overall (HPDv2 43.34%, Pick-a-Pic 40.08%), followed by East Asian and Indian; some verbs show exceptions (e.g., “bake” favors Black, “fish” favors East Asian). The section argues these biases may propagate into reward-model training and downstream video generation. It then begins constructing a benchmark for evaluating reward models using T2I generation with FLUX and event prompting templates, with two settings: Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender, generating 100 images per prompt.

Section 5 now details the benchmark for image reward models. Table 3 lists prompt counts: Ethnicity+Person has 294 prompts; Ethnicity+Gender has 1176 prompts. The authors use FLUX only as a controlled/reproducible generator, then verify benchmark integrity with 3 annotators on 100 sampled images: 77% unanimous agreement, 97% majority agreement, and only 3 images lacking consensus. Figure 5 shows example prompts of the form “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context],” with shown genders limited to man/woman.

They evaluate four reward models: HPSv2.0 (trained on HPDv2), HPSv2.1 (trained on HPDv2.1), PickScore (trained on Pick-a-Pic), and CLIP as the common base model. Scores are continuous preference values. Table 4 reports bias metrics across 42 verbs: ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG), ethnic representation distribution (RDS), and overall SDI.

Main results in Table 4: CLIP has average PBSG -0.0726 and SDI 0.8495. HPSv2.0 shows strong positive average PBSG 0.6039 with SDI 0.8492. HPSv2.1 has average PBSG -0.0984 with SDI 0.8470. PickScore has average PBSG -0.1157 with SDI 0.8483.

Section 5 continues with two bias analyses. For ethnicity-aware gender bias, evaluation prompts are of the form “A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]” (ethnicity+person), while generation prompts are “A/An [ethnicity] [gender] is [verb]-ing [context]” (ethnicity+gender). The gender is omitted only in evaluation prompts to probe the reward model’s preference. Reward scores are standardized, averaged over 100 images per generation prompt, and PBSG is computed by fixing ethnicity and verb and subtracting women’s average standardized score from men’s. PBSG can exceed 1; positive means male preference, negative means female preference. Reported PBSG means: CLIP −0.0726 (slight woman preference), HPSv2.0 +0.6039 (strong man preference), HPSv2.1 −0.0984, PickScore −0.1157. The text says these patterns are consistent across ethnic groups and figures 19–25 show PBSG across 42 verbs.

For ethnicity bias, evaluation prompts are “A person is [verb]-ing [context]” (person-only), while generation prompts are “A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]” (ethnicity+person). Scores are standardized, then RDSe and SDI are computed by fixing the verb and applying softmax across ethnicities. Positive RDSe indicates overrepresentation; higher SDI means more balanced/diverse outputs. CLIP slightly favors White individuals (RDS 0.0182) and has the highest SDI 0.8495. Two reward models are trained from the same pretrained Y2F encoder: Z6B = Man-Preferred Reward Model (RMM) and P3L = Woman-Preferred Reward Model (RMW).

Table 7 reports reward-model L2V bias across 42 verbs. Y2F is near zero overall (-0.0726). Z6B strongly increases scores (Average 1.5280, with all demographic groups around 1.43–1.63), while P3L strongly decreases them (Average -0.7448, with all demographic groups around -0.63 to -0.88). The text says Z6B raises gender preference scores across groups, while P3L systematically favors women.

Table 8 reports aligned-video-model L2V social bias for G4S, +Z6B, and +P3L. G4S Average is 0.8034; +Z6B increases it to 0.9584 across all demographics; +P3L reduces it to 0.3082. The narrative says Z6B reinforces man preference, P3L shifts toward woman preference, and that directionally biased reward tuning can correct imbalance. Figure 6 analyzes action-level sensitivity, noting that Z6B amplifies male-preferred actions like exercise, row, and cook, while P3L shifts bake, sleep, and sweep toward women; sleep, stretch, and read are most sensitive under both directions.

Conclusion/limitations: the paper argues bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation. It notes predefined gender/ethnicity categories are limited and future work should include intersectional groups; VLM judges are image-level and imperfect; current alignment experiments use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation is only targeted modulation and does not solve broader value alignment; and the fixed action taxonomy limits open-ended generalization.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. Two conditions are defined: Person-only (42 prompts, one per verb) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities). Table 1 gives prompt counts/examples. Here, gender bias is operationalized only with binary labels man/woman via PBSG, while ethnicity uses seven groups and metrics RDS_e and SDI. Section 4 evaluates four video diffusion models in two aligned–unaligned pairs: ModelScope vs InstructVideo, and VideoCrafter-2 vs T2V-Turbo-V1. For each prompt, each model generates 10 videos with different seeds; results are averaged over 42 verbs. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI). Across all ethnic groups, average PBSG is positive (male-preference), and alignment increases this bias for both pairs: ModelScope 0.4815→0.5295 (+0.0480) and VideoCrafter-2 0.7581→0.8306 (+0.0725). Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. The VLM ensemble correlates with human judgments at Pearson 0.89 (gender) and 0.73 (ethnicity); agreement is strong, with Cohen’s Kappa 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ Kappa 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. A high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions yields stable bias metrics: PBSG 0.846→0.863 (p=0.68) and SDI 0.745→0.761. The paper argues remaining ethnicity disagreements often reflect human holistic judgment vs frame-level precision, especially fleeting faces.

Introduction defines “aligned models” as video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, contrasted with unaligned likelihood-only baselines. VideoBiasEval evaluates bias by varying actor gender and ethnicity across 42 socially associated verbs in real-world event prompts, then extracting attributes from generated videos. An event is a tuple <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. The verb list is: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. Two conditions are defined: Person-only (42 prompts, one per verb) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities). Table 1 gives prompt counts/examples. The paper says Ethnicity+Person already isolates ethnicity effects, so no separate ethnicity-only condition is used.

Human evaluation uses 3 independent annotators on 400 videos, with training and written guidelines. Majority-vote ensemble vs human judgments: Pearson 0.89 (gender), 0.73 (ethnicity). Inter-annotator agreement: Cohen’s kappa 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ kappa 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. A high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions has consensus rates 99.0% (gender) and 83.3% (ethnicity); PBSG changes 0.846→0.863 (p=0.68) and SDI 0.745→0.761, so residual evaluator uncertainty does not materially affect measurements.

Section 5 studies bias in image reward data and reward models as a source for video alignment bias. In 5.1, HPDv2 has 28,783 validated (image, caption, preference) tuples covering 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs. GPT-4o-mini extracts gender/ethnicity/verbs from captions, and Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B classify image attributes. For gender, 26/42 verbs in HPDv2 have valid man–woman pairs, with 69.23% (18/26) favoring men; in Pick-a-Pic, 18/42 qualify, with 61.11% (11/18) favoring women. For ethnicity, White representations are most preferred overall: 43.34% in HPDv2 and 40.08% in Pick-a-Pic, followed by East Asian and Indian; some verbs differ (e.g., “bake” favors Black individuals, “fish” favors East Asians). The section argues these biases may propagate into reward models. In 5.2, they build a controlled text-to-image benchmark using FLUX and event templates from Section 3.2, with two settings: Ethnicity+Person and Ethnicity+Gender. They generate 100 images per prompt; Table 3 reports 294 prompts for Ethnicity+Person and 1176 for Ethnicity+Gender.

This part reports annotation quality for the benchmark: 100 randomly sampled images were reviewed by three annotators; 77% had unanimous agreement, 97% had majority agreement, and only three lacked consensus. The preference-bias evaluation compares four reward models: HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore, and CLIP. Table 4 reports average PBSG, per-ethnicity PBSG/RDS, and overall SDI across 42 verbs. For gender bias, CLIP shows a slight woman preference (-0.0726), HPSv2.0 shows strong man preference (+0.6039), and both HPSv2.1 (-0.0984) and PickScore (-0.1157) favor women overall. For ethnicity bias, CLIP slightly favors White individuals (RDS 0.0182) and has the highest SDI (0.8495). After fine-tuning, HPSv2.0 favors Middle Eastern representation (RDS 0.0315), HPSv2.1 favors Latino representation (RDS 0.0382), and PickScore favors East Asian representation (RDS 0.0352); all fine-tuned models have lower SDI than CLIP.

Section 7 explores controllable preference modeling for gender bias in video diffusion. It constructs two preference datasets from the Ethnicity+Gender set: a man-preferred set and a woman-preferred set, each with 2.94 million same-action, same-ethnicity pairs, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Male images are labeled 1 in the man-preferred set and 0 in the woman-preferred set, with labels reversed for women.

Two reward models are fine-tuned: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 shows RMM scores are much higher than CLIP across all demographic groups (average 1.5280), while RMW scores are much lower (average -0.7448), indicating the models learn opposite gender preferences. The paper then aligns VCM-VC2 with each reward model. Table 8 shows RMM increases PBSG from 0.8034 to 0.9584 across all ethnic groups, reinforcing male preference, while RMW lowers PBSG to 0.3082 across all groups, counteracting the base model’s male bias. The section’s conclusion is that deliberately skewed reward data can steer video-model gender portrayals in either direction, and counter-biased RMW yields more balanced outputs.

Section 7 continues on controllable preference modeling for gender bias in video diffusion. It builds man-preferred and woman-preferred preference datasets from the Ethnicity+Gender set (2.94M same-action, same-ethnicity pairs each) plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Labels are assigned so male images are preferred in the man-preferred set and female images in the woman-preferred set, with the opposite labeling in the other set.

Two reward models are fine-tuned: RMM and RMW. Table 7 shows RMM scores are positive and much higher than CLIP on average (1.5280), while RMW scores are negative on average (-0.7448), indicating opposite learned preferences. Aligning VCM-VC2 with RMM raises PBSG from 0.8034 to 0.9584 across ethnic groups; aligning with RMW lowers PBSG to 0.3082 across all groups, counteracting the base model’s male bias.

Figure 6 analyzes action-level sensitivity to alignment. RMM especially amplifies male-preferred portrayals for exercise, row, and cook; RMW shifts bake, sleep, and sweep toward women-preferred portrayals. The most sensitive actions under both directions are sleep, stretch, and read. The section concludes that bias can be steered in either direction via reward-data composition, and action-level audits are useful. It also adds a responsible-use caveat and suggests mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data may offer a continuous control axis, though that mixture idea is framed as a suggestion rather than a reported experiment.

Section 8 concludes that VideoBiasEval exposes blind spots in text-to-video social-bias evaluation by separating identity attributes from content semantics and tracking how alignment changes representation. It emphasizes that reward-based alignment inherits and can amplify human-preference bias, while also noting that reward design can counter existing bias. The conclusion cites: HPDv2 verbs favor men 69.23% (18/26), Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women 61.11% (11/18), HPSv2.0 average PBSG 0.6039, PickScore -0.1157, VCM-VC2 0.8034, +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082), and +RMW 0.3082.

Section 9 (Limitations) says the paper’s findings are limited by five factors: (1) use of predefined gender/ethnicity categories from U.S. Census conventions and prior work, which miss fluid/intersectional identities; (2) VLM evaluators that still rely on image-level classification and may be biased/inaccurate on stylized or ambiguous frames, though ensembling helps; (3) experiments mainly use single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models, leaving RL-based tuning and multi-turn video instruction alignment unexplored; (4) controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations and do not address broader value-alignment or societal-impact questions; and (5) VideoBiasEval uses a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalization to open-ended generation or novel actions. No contradictions with earlier sections noted.

Section 10 (Broader Impact Statement) argues that alignment can stabilize and entrench bias in video diffusion models. It says RLHF-style tuning can improve fidelity and temporal consistency while also making stereotypes appear more natural and authoritative. It emphasizes dual use of preference control: the same method can mitigate or intensify representational harm through curated reward data. It recommends ongoing auditing of social composition with multi-granular, event-centric tools like VideoBiasEval and careful, equitable preference-data curation.

final_notes: Section 7 studied controllable preference modeling by altering gender composition in preference data to steer reward models and then a video diffusion model (VCM-VC2). The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework for measuring social bias in video generation. It defines each event as a tuple ⟨p,a,c⟩: actor p, verb a, context c. The framework uses structured prompts that vary gender and ethnicity across real-world events, then generates videos with diffusion models and evaluates social-attribute consistency/fairness from the outputs. final_notes:
Section 7 studies controllable gender preference modeling for video diffusion. It builds two image reward datasets from C4Z, each with 29.4M preference pairs fixing action and ethnicity while varying gender, plus 537,660 extra pairs for face-free diversity. Man-preferred labels mark male images as 1 and female as 0; woman-preferred labels reverse this. Two reward models are trained from the same pretrained Y2F encoder: Z6B (man-preferred reward model, RMM) and P3L (woman-preferred reward model, RMW).

Table 7: baseline Y2F average -0.0726; Z6B average 1.5280 across groups; P3L average -0.7448, with all subgroup scores negative. The text says Z6B consistently raises gender preference scores, while P3L systematically favors women.

Table 8: G4S baseline average social-bias L2V is 0.8034. +Z6B raises it to 0.9584 across all demographics. +P3L lowers it to 0.3082 across all demographics. The narrative says Z6B reinforces man preference and P3L strongly shifts toward woman preference, framing P3L as a corrective, analogous to U8D in section 6.

Figure 6/action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies male-preferred exercise, row, and cook; P3L shifts bake, sleep, and sweep toward women. Sleep, stretch, and read are highest-sensitivity actions under both reward directions. Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation, and notes limits from predefined categories, human VLM judge bias, single-step alignment experiments, synthetic gender manipulation, and fixed action taxonomies.

Broader impact statement: alignment can stabilize and entrench bias; preference data can be used for both bias correction and exclusionary propaganda; developers should monitor generated social composition with multi-granular audits like QX2. Supplementary inventory lists additional gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, statistical analyses, reward-model implementation/training details, video post-training/inference details, and multiple numbered plots for gender and ethnicity across 42 verbs/actions and across reward-model, aligned-video, and controllable-preference settings.

The paper argues that biases in human preference data are learned by reward models, amplified, and then propagated into video generation. It introduces QX2, an event-based benchmark that separates verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, and measures: (1) ethnic skew, (2) ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, (3) cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and (4) within-video persistence. Claimed contribution: first end-to-end analysis linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing that human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality while unintentionally encoding and amplifying social bias.

Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core thesis: alignment-tuned video diffusion models improve perceptual quality/smoothness but also produce more stereotyped and temporally persistent social portrayals. The paper argues that human preference data contain social biases that are learned by reward models, amplified, and then propagated into video generation.

Main setup: an event-based benchmark called QX2 (also referred to as VideoBiasEval) separates semantic content (verbs/events/contexts) from actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity, enabling controlled comparison across 42 events. Reported bias measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video temporal persistence.

Claimed contributions: (1) a comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit of bias in aligned video diffusion; (2) the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance and amplification of bias; and (3) evidence that alignment can simultaneously improve visual quality/coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing social composition, plus guidance via controlled/counter-biased preference data for mitigation. The introduction emphasizes that unaligned models are likelihood-only baselines, while aligned models are post-trained with reward/preference optimization.

Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core thesis: alignment-tuned video diffusion models improve perceptual quality/smoothness but also produce more stereotyped and temporally persistent social portrayals. The paper argues that human preference data contain social biases that are learned by reward models, amplified, and then propagated into video generation.

Main setup: an event-based benchmark called QX2 (also referred to as VideoBiasEval) separates semantic content (verbs/events/contexts) from actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity, enabling controlled comparison across 42 events. Prompt settings include J7K (person-only, 42 prompts) and V9R (ethnicity+person, 294 prompts) across 7 ethnic groups. Reported bias measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video temporal persistence.

Key metrics: L2V (PBSG) = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total in [-1,1], where positive values favor men and negative values favor women; gender-only analysis is excluded because absent specified ethnicity the model predominantly depicts White individuals. Ethnic quantities include P_e = N_e/N_total, F6N_e (RDS_e) = P_e - 1/|E|, and W3H (SDI) = 1 - sum_e P_e^2; higher W3H means more diverse/balanced output. Shift metrics are ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, and ΔW3H, with more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, or higher diversity treated as improvement.

Claimed contributions: (1) a comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit of bias in aligned video diffusion; (2) the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance and amplification of bias; and (3) evidence that alignment can simultaneously improve visual quality/coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing social composition, plus guidance via controlled/counter-biased preference data for mitigation.

final_notes:
Section 9 (Limitations) says the paper’s main limitations are: identity analysis is restricted to predefined U.S. Census-style gender and ethnicity categories; the human-validated VLM evaluators are image-level classifiers that may be biased/inaccurate, especially on stylized or ambiguous frames; the main intervention tested is single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models, so other tuning protocols (e.g., RL or multi-turn instruction alignment) could behave differently; the controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations and do not address broader value-alignment or societal-impact questions; and VideoBiasEval covers a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions, which may limit generalization to open-ended or novel actions.

Broader Impact Statement argues that alignment can stabilize and entrench bias by making stereotypes look more natural and authoritative. It also says the preference-control method is dual-use: it can mitigate or intensify representational harm depending on curated preference data, potentially leading to exclusion, homogenization, or propaganda. Evidence cited: Table 5 average PBSG for VCM-VC2 0.8034 vs +HPSv2.0 0.9116; Table 6 gender rows mean TAS 0.9763→0.9967 and perfect stability 0.8850→0.9830; Table 7 average reward PBSG RMM 1.5280 and RMW -0.7448; Table 8 average video PBSG +RMM 0.9584 and +RMW 0.3082.

The paper’s notation section defines event tuples <p,a,c> for actor/verb/context. It uses p for the actor, a for the verb, c for context, g for gender label, and e for ethnicity label. G is the two-label gender output set {man, woman}; E is the seven-ethnicity evaluation set, with |E| the number of groups. Metrics: PBSG (gender proportion bias score) is a video-count difference divided by total, or in reward-model evaluation a standardized reward-score difference; RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|, with RDSWhite as the White-specific value; SDI = 1 - sum_e P_e^2; TAS is the percentage of frames matching the video’s final majority-voted attribute label; Δ denotes alignment-induced change in a metric. Prompt/template categories include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and a note that Ethnicity-only is discussed in Section 6 even though Section 3.2 says it is unnecessary. Gender prompt categories include Man, Woman, Person, and Non-binary person. The seven ethnicity groups are White, Black, Indian/India (table label), East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The 42 evaluated verbs are listed. The section also mentions M-1/W-1 preference-pair example labels and RM_M / RM_W as the man-preferred and woman-preferred reward models.

Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. The paper argues remaining ethnicity disagreements often reflect human holistic judgment vs frame-level precision, especially fleeting faces.

Introduction defines “aligned models” as video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, contrasted with unaligned likelihood-only baselines. Related work argues that existing T2V benchmarks and bias evaluations focus on surface-level or per-image metrics and overlook who is depicted, what roles they occupy, and how biases unfold across events or narratives; the paper positions its event-centric framework as addressing this gap.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework for measuring social bias in video generation. It defines each event as a tuple ⟨p,a,c⟩: actor p, verb a, context c. The framework uses structured prompts that vary gender and ethnicity across real-world events, then generates videos with diffusion models and evaluates social-attribute consistency/fairness from the outputs. The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 socially associated verbs (e.g., bake, bike, clean, cook, drive, read, run, walk). The section emphasizes that this bounded setup is meant to support reproducible, interpretable bias analysis and the first end-to-end tracing of bias propagation in video generation.

final_notes:
Section 8 gives a broader impact statement: widespread deployment can entrench bias; alignment/RLHF may stabilize stereotypes by removing artifacts; curated preference data is dual-use for mitigation or exclusion/propaganda; and developers should monitor generated social composition with multi-granular audits like QX2. It reiterates that aesthetic metrics alone are insufficient and that preference-data curation should aim at a diverse, equitable society.

The supplementary inventory lists supporting materials: A (additional 42-verb video analysis, WebVid-10M training-data effects, statistical analysis 9), a dataset ethnicity item numbered 10 (human image-reward-dataset ethnicity distributions), C (reward-model implementation, comprehensive 42-verb analysis, statistical analysis 11), D (additional 42-verb aligned-video analysis, statistical analysis 12), F (reward-model training/inference details), G (video post-training/inference details), plus multiple gender and ethnicity plots for four-model L2V, reward-model bias, aligned-video bias, and controllable-preference analyses across 42 verbs/actions by ethnicity.

Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core thesis: alignment-tuned video diffusion models improve perceptual quality/smoothness but also produce more stereotyped and temporally persistent social portrayals. The paper argues that human preference data contain social biases that are learned by reward models, amplified, and then propagated into video generation.

Main setup: an event-based benchmark called QX2 (also referred to as VideoBiasEval) separates semantic content (verbs/events/contexts) from actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity, enabling controlled comparison across 42 events. Prompt settings include J7K (person-only, 42 prompts) and V9R (ethnicity+person, 294 prompts) across 7 ethnic groups. Reported bias measures include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video temporal persistence.

Key metrics: L2V (PBSG) = (N_man - N_woman)/N_total in [-1,1], where positive values favor men and negative values favor women; gender-only analysis is excluded because absent specified ethnicity the model predominantly depicts White individuals. Ethnic quantities include P_e = N_e/N_total, F6N_e (RDS_e) = P_e - 1/|E|, and W3H (SDI) = 1 - sum_e P_e^2; higher W3H means more diverse/balanced output. Shift metrics are ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, and ΔW3H, with more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, or higher diversity treated as improvement.

Claimed contributions: (1) a comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity audit of bias in aligned video diffusion; (2) the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned rewards, and aligned video outputs, showing inheritance and amplification of bias; and (3) evidence that alignment can simultaneously improve visual quality/coherence while reshaping and sometimes reinforcing social composition, plus guidance via controlled/counter-biased preference data for mitigation.

Section 5 discusses social biases in image reward datasets and learned reward models. In 5.1, R9C (HPDv2) has 28,783 validated tuples, 29 covered verbs, 26 valid man–woman-pair verbs, men preferred in 69.23% (18/26), White preference 43.34%; N6T (Pick-a-Pic) has 14,958 tuples, 19 covered verbs, 18 valid pair verbs, women preferred in 61.11% (11/18), White preference 40.08%. Both datasets favor White over East Asian and Indian; exceptions mentioned: Black preference for “bake” and East Asian preference for “fish.”

Table 4 compares reward models Y2F, A3J, U8D, E5W (with Δ rows for fine-tuning shifts). Y2F has average L2V -0.0726 and W3H 0.8495; A3J 0.6039 and 0.8492; U8D -0.0984 and 0.8470; E5W -0.1157 and 0.8483. White F6N values: Y2F 0.0182, A3J -0.0423, U8D -0.0189, E5W 0.0069. Narrative says Y2F slightly favors women and White individuals; A3J shows strong man preference; U8D and E5W favor women. Fine-tuned ethnic preferences are said to shift toward Middle Eastern in A3J, Latino in U8D, and East Asian in E5W.

Benchmark construction: controlled T2I benchmark uses FLUX and event templates to vary gender, ethnicity, and verbs. C4Z = Ethnicity+Gender; V9R = ethnicity alone; both generate 100 images per prompt.

Section 5.1/Table 3 describe the controlled image-reward benchmark. V9R has 294 prompts (ethnicity only) and C4Z has 1176 prompts (ethnicity + gender); example prompts are baking scenes with explicit ethnicity/and gender when applicable. The benchmark uses FLUX, but the authors do not assume it is unbiased. Three annotators reviewed 100 random images: 77% had unanimous agreement and 97% had majority confirmation, with only three lacking consensus; disagreements were attributed to ambiguous visuals, not systematic demographic issues.

Figure 5 describes constructed images with the template “A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context],” with gender restricted to man/woman.

Reward identities: Y2F = CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), A3J = HPSv2.0 trained on R9C (Wu et al., 2023), U8D = HPSv2.1 (Wu et al., 2023) trained on X7H = HPDv2.1, and E5W = PickScore trained on N6T (Kirstain et al., 2023b). Scores are continuous scalar preference values, standardized by mean/std and averaged per prompt. For gender, adapted L2V is computed as men’s standardized score minus women’s; it can exceed 1. For ethnicity, standardized prompt scores are softmax-normalized across ethnicities to yield preference distributions.

Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation. Limitations: categories are socially constructed and miss intersectionality; VLM judges are image-level and imperfect; experiments are limited to single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender manipulation does not solve broader value alignment; and the fixed action taxonomy limits open-ended generalization.

Section 10 (Broader Impact Statement) argues that alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, and that preference control is dual-use. It says polished outputs can make stereotypes seem more natural, coherent, and authoritative. It recommends continuous auditing with multi-granular event-centric frameworks such as VideoBiasEval and says aesthetic metrics alone are insufficient.

steps.notes_before: Section 3.3 introduces multi-granular event-centric bias evaluation using three open-source VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B). They uniformly sample 16 frames per video and first majority-vote frame labels to get video-level labels, then fuse across models. Frame/video analysis covers temporal attribute stability (TAS), gender bias, ethnicity bias, and bias shifts between aligned and unaligned models. Here, gender bias is operationalized only with binary labels man/woman via PBSG, while ethnicity uses seven groups and metrics RDS_e and SDI. A footnote says gender-only analysis is omitted because without explicit ethnicity specifications models mostly produce White individuals, so gender-alone analysis would mainly reflect White demographic bias.

Section 4 evaluates four video diffusion models in two aligned–unaligned pairs: ModelScope vs InstructVideo, and VideoCrafter-2 vs T2V-Turbo-V1. For each prompt, each model generates 10 videos with different seeds; results are averaged over 42 verbs. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI). Across all ethnic groups, average PBSG is positive (male-preference), and alignment increases this bias for both pairs: ModelScope 0.4815→0.5295 (+0.0480) and VideoCrafter-2 0.7581→0.8306 (+0.0725). Under person-only prompts, all models overrepresent White individuals; ModelScope has the strongest White dominance (RDSWhite 0.7690, SDI 0.0538), InstructVideo is slightly worse (0.7833, 0.0267), while VideoCrafter-2 is less skewed (0.6905, 0.1252) and T2V-Turbo-V1 further lowers White RDS to 0.6381 but also lowers SDI to 0.1119. Missing RDS values (“—”) occur for some ethnicities when no recognizable instances appear under person-only prompts.

Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. final_notes: Section 8 concludes that the paper’s main contribution is VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in text-to-video generation by decoupling identity attributes from content semantics and tracking how alignment tuning changes social representations. It argues that reward-model-based alignment often inherits and amplifies biases from human preference data, motivating bias auditing and mitigation throughout the video generation pipeline. The Limitations section says the study covers only gender and ethnicity using U.S. Census-style predefined categories, relies on VLM-based image-level evaluators that may have their own biases, focuses on single-step latent consistency distillation and a limited set of reward models, uses only synthetic gender-preference manipulations in controllable preference modeling, and benchmarks VideoBiasEval on a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions. The Broader Impact statement adds that alignment tuning can act as a “bias stabilizer” by making stereotyped depictions appear more natural and authoritative, and that controllable preference modeling is dual-use because curated preference datasets can be used to amplify or suppress social attributes, supporting both fairness and exclusionary or propaganda uses. The acknowledgment adds funding/support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, and the Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving.

It emphasizes this is a parity baseline for controlled bias auditing, not a claim about real-world demographics. The paper also defines Simpson’s Diversity Index (SDI) = 1 - sum_e P_e^2, where higher SDI means more diverse/balanced representation. final_notes:
Section 7 presents controllable preference modeling for gender in image/video alignment. It builds two 2.94M-pair C4Z preference datasets plus 537,660 R9C pairs, using prompts like “A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].” Man-preferred labels assign male images 1; woman-preferred labels reverse that. The reward models are Z6B (Man-Preferred Reward Model, RMM) and P3L (Woman-Preferred Reward Model, RMW).

Table 7 reports reward-model L2V bias: baseline Y2F average -0.0726; Z6B average 1.5280 across groups; P3L average -0.7448 across groups. The text says Z6B reinforces male preference and P3L systematically favors women.

Table 8 reports aligned-video-model L2V social bias: baseline G4S average 0.8034; +Z6B raises it to 0.9584 across all demographics; +P3L lowers it to 0.3082 across all demographics. The prose says Z6B reinforces man preference, P3L shifts toward woman preference, and no neutral reward is trained.

Figure 6 shows action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies male-preferred exercise, row, and cook; P3L shifts bake, sleep, and sweep toward women. Sleep, stretch, and read are highest-sensitivity actions under both directions. The section ends with a responsible-use warning.

Section 8 concludes that bias auditing and mitigation should be integrated throughout video generation. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories are practical but socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality; VLM judges are image-level classifiers with possible biases; alignment experiments use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation does not address broader value alignment or societal impact; and the fixed action taxonomy limits generalization to open-ended or novel actions. The broader impact statement adds that alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, preference data can be dual-use, and continual auditing is necessary.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 defines QX2 as an event-based audit pipeline for structured-event videos. An event is ⟨p,a,c⟩ with actor, verb, and context. The curated space is 42 verbs, 7 ethnic groups, and (claimed) 4 gender categories: man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person. The prompt protocol has two settings: J7K (42 prompts, person-only) and V9R (294 prompts, ethnicity+person). J7K leaves actor demographics implicit; V9R prepends an explicit ethnicity to person. Evaluation uses 3 VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B), 16 sampled frames per video, within-model majority vote, then fusion across models. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) is the percentage of frames matching the video’s final majority-voted label.

Section 4 defines bias metrics. Conditional gender quantity: L2V (PBSG) is (N_man - N_woman)/N_total with N_total = N_man + N_woman, so it only uses man/woman counts; positive means male-skew, negative female-skew. It is computed under the ethnicity+gender condition to study ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes. The paper says gender-only analysis is excluded because prompts without ethnicity mostly produce White individuals, so that setting effectively measures White-group gender bias. Ethnic quantities: P_e = N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnicity outputs; F6N_e (RDS_e) = P_e - 1/|E| with uniform reference 1/7 for the neutral J7K audit; W3H (SDI) = 1 - sum_e P_e^2. Higher W3H means more diverse/balanced; lower means more concentrated. Shift quantities are delta L2V, delta F6N_e, and delta W3H; improvements are more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, and higher diversity.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. final_notes: Section 7 concludes that controllable preference modeling can steer gender bias in video diffusion models through reward-dataset composition. A man-preferred reward model (RMM) amplifies male-preferred portrayals, while a woman-preferred reward model (RMW) counteracts them. The paper frames this as a continuous alignment axis: mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data trade off bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence. Figure 6 shows action-level PBSG changes before vs. after alignment tuning with RMM and RMW. Actions cluster by the guiding reward model: RMM increases male-preferred portrayals for actions like exercise, row, and cook, whereas RMW shifts outputs toward women-preferred actions like bake, sleep, and sweep. Figures 6(b) and 6(c) rank actions by normalized sensitivity (ΔPBSG divided by baseline PBSG), and sleep, stretch, and read are among the most sensitive actions under both tuning directions. The section emphasizes that even neutral or domestic activities can show large gender shifts under alignment. The responsible-use paragraph argues that controllable preference modeling is not a silver bullet and should be guided by stakeholder/community input rather than automated optimization alone. The broader impact statement adds that alignment tuning may act as a "bias stabilizer," making stereotyped portrayals appear more natural and authoritative, and emphasizes the dual-use risk of controllable preference modeling. It recommends multi-granular, event-centric auditing with VideoBiasEval and careful preference-dataset curation. Section 8 concludes that VideoBiasEval provides a comprehensive framework for decoupling identity attributes from content semantics and tracking how alignment tuning reshapes social representations; it summarizes the main finding that reward-model-based alignment inherits and often amplifies biases in human preference data. The limitations section adds that the study focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses predefined U.S.-Census-style categories, relies on VLM-based evaluators, studies only single-step latent consistency distillation and a limited set of reward models, and benchmarks VideoBiasEval on 42 socially associated actions.
