Introduction defines “aligned models” as video diffusion models post-trained beyond likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, contrasted with unaligned likelihood-only baselines. Alignment is described as reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization using preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. The paper argues that preference data may encode social biases that downstream aligned generators inherit, motivating the question of how alignment changes social-attribute distributions in video models. It claims prior evaluation frameworks are insufficient because they use non-diverse prompts, lack comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and do not track before-vs-after alignment shifts. The paper focuses on gender and ethnicity. It proposes multi-granular metrics for (1) ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distribution shifts across models, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos.

The paper first examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic, then checks whether image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore) inherit those preferences, and finally fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 with these reward models to study before-vs-after alignment. The reported findings are that both preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and strong White favoritism; reward models inherit and amplify these biases; and alignment tuning shifts gender portrayals while ethnic representation remains uneven. Paper: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main thesis in abstract: alignment-tuned video diffusion models produce smoother outputs but also more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Shift metrics are ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, and ΔW3H, with more balanced gender ratios, less ethnic skew, or higher diversity treated as improvement.

final_notes: Section 8’s broader impact statement argues that video diffusion alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, making stereotypes look more natural and authoritative. It frames the work’s main safety lesson as dual use: the same preference-control methods can either mitigate or intensify representational harm, so auditing and curation are needed throughout the pipeline. The section cites evidence that alignment can increase bias stability: Table 5 shows Average PBSG for VCM-VC2 rising from 0.8034 to 0.9116 under HPSv2.0, and Table 6 shows gender mean TAS increasing from 0.9763 to 0.9967 and perfect stability from 0.8850 to 0.9830. The section explicitly warns about normalization, exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda as potential risks. The final acknowledgment thanks reviewers and lists support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, and the Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving, with a standard disclaimer that conclusions do not represent those organizations.

VideoBiasEval evaluates bias by varying actor gender and ethnicity across 42 socially associated verbs in real-world event prompts, then extracting attributes from generated videos. An event is a tuple <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. The verb list is: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. Two conditions are defined: Person-only (42 prompts, one per verb) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities). Table 1 gives prompt counts/examples. The paper says Ethnicity+Person already isolates ethnicity effects, so no separate ethnicity-only condition is used.

Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. The VLM ensemble correlates with human judgments at Pearson 0.89 (gender) and 0.73 (ethnicity); agreement is strong, with Cohen’s Kappa 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ Kappa 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. A high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions yields stable bias metrics: PBSG 0.846→0.863 (p=0.68) and SDI 0.745→0.761. The paper argues remaining ethnicity disagreements often reflect human holistic judgment vs frame-level precision, especially fleeting faces.

Section 5 studies social bias in image reward datasets and reward models. It analyzes HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic using GPT-4o-mini caption extraction plus Qwen2-VL/Qwen2.5-VL/InternVL2.5 image classification, keeping tuples with predefined verbs. After processing, HPDv2 has 28,783 validated tuples covering 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs. For gender preference, 26 of 42 verbs in HPDv2 have valid man–woman pairs and 69.23% (18/26) favor men; Pick-a-Pic has 18/42 qualifying verbs and 61.11% (11/18) favor women. For ethnicity, White representations are most preferred overall: 43.34% in HPDv2 and 40.08% in Pick-a-Pic; East Asian and Indian follow. Example verbs include “bake” favoring Black individuals and “fish” favoring East Asians. The section argues these preference imbalances may transmit into reward models and downstream alignment.

Figure 6 analyzes action-level sensitivity under alignment. RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals for actions such as exercise, row, and cook; RMW shifts actions such as bake, sleep, and sweep toward women-preferred portrayals. Sleep, stretch, and read are the most sensitive under both directions. The section also emphasizes responsible use and stakeholder consultation for representation goals.

The paper’s notation section defines event tuples <p,a,c> for actor/verb/context. It uses p for the actor, a for the verb, c for context, g for gender label, and e for ethnicity label. G is the two-label gender output set {man, woman}; E is the seven-ethnicity evaluation set, with |E| the number of groups. Metrics: PBSG (gender proportion bias score) is a video-count difference divided by total, or in reward-model evaluation a standardized reward-score difference; RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|, with RDSWhite as the White-specific value; SDI = 1 - sum_e P_e^2; TAS is the percentage of frames matching the video’s final majority-voted attribute label; Δ denotes alignment-induced change in a metric. Prompt/template categories include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and a note that Ethnicity-only is discussed in Section 6 even though Section 3.2 says it is unnecessary. Gender prompt categories include Man, Woman, Person, and Non-binary person. The seven ethnicity groups are White, Black, Indian/India (table label), East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The 42 evaluated verbs are listed. The section also mentions M-1/W-1 preference-pair example labels and RM_M / RM_W as the man-preferred and woman-preferred reward models.

VideoBiasEval evaluates bias by varying actor gender and ethnicity across 42 socially associated verbs in real-world event prompts, then extracting attributes from generated videos. An event is a tuple <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). Controlled attribute space: 4 gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), 7 ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. The verb list is: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work.

Prompting protocol uses deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; no LLM-generated prompts at runtime. Two conditions are defined: Person-only (42 prompts, one per verb) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities). Table 1 gives prompt counts/examples. The paper says Ethnicity+Person already isolates ethnicity effects, so no separate ethnicity-only condition is used.

steps.notes_before: Section 3.3 introduces multi-granular event-centric bias evaluation using three open-source VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B). They uniformly sample 16 frames per video and first majority-vote frame labels to get video-level labels, then fuse across models. Frame/video analysis covers temporal attribute stability (TAS), gender bias, ethnicity bias, and bias shifts between aligned and unaligned models. Here, gender bias is operationalized only with binary labels man/woman via PBSG, while ethnicity uses seven groups and metrics RDS_e and SDI. A footnote says gender-only analysis is omitted because without explicit ethnicity specifications models mostly produce White individuals, so gender-alone analysis would mainly reflect White demographic bias.

Section 4 evaluates four video diffusion models in two aligned–unaligned pairs: ModelScope vs InstructVideo, and VideoCrafter-2 vs T2V-Turbo-V1. For each prompt, each model generates 10 videos with different seeds; results are averaged over 42 verbs. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI). Across all ethnic groups, average PBSG is positive (male-preference), and alignment increases this bias for both pairs: ModelScope 0.4815→0.5295 (+0.0480) and VideoCrafter-2 0.7581→0.8306 (+0.0725). Under person-only prompts, all models overrepresent White individuals; ModelScope has the strongest White dominance (RDSWhite 0.7690, SDI 0.0538), InstructVideo is slightly worse (0.7833, 0.0267), while VideoCrafter-2 is less skewed (0.6905, 0.1252) and T2V-Turbo-V1 further lowers White RDS to 0.6381 but also lowers SDI to 0.1119. Missing RDS values (“—”) occur for some ethnicities when no recognizable instances appear under person-only prompts.

Human evaluation verifies gender and ethnicity in 400 generated videos using three independent annotators. The VLM ensemble correlates with human judgments at Pearson 0.89 (gender) and 0.73 (ethnicity); agreement is strong, with Cohen’s Kappa 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ Kappa 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. A high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions yields stable bias metrics: PBSG 0.846→0.863 (p=0.68) and SDI 0.745→0.761. The paper argues remaining ethnicity disagreements often reflect human holistic judgment vs frame-level precision, especially fleeting faces.

Section 5 studies social bias in image reward datasets and reward models. It analyzes HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic using GPT-4o-mini caption extraction plus Qwen2-VL/Qwen2.5-VL/InternVL2.5 image classification, keeping tuples with predefined verbs. After processing, HPDv2 has 28,783 validated tuples covering 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples covering 19 verbs. For gender preference, 26 of 42 verbs in HPDv2 have valid man–woman pairs and 69.23% (18/26) favor men; Pick-a-Pic has 18/42 qualifying verbs and 61.11% (11/18) favor women. For ethnicity, White representations are most preferred overall: 43.34% in HPDv2 and 40.08% in Pick-a-Pic; East Asian and Indian follow. Example verbs include “bake” favoring Black individuals and “fish” favoring East Asians. The section argues these preference imbalances may transmit into reward models and downstream alignment.

Section 5.2 constructs a controlled text-to-image benchmark using FLUX and event templates from Section 3.2, with two settings: Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts) and Ethnicity+Gender (1176 prompts). The benchmark varies ethnicity, gender, and verb, and generates 100 images per prompt. The section emphasizes the benchmark is controlled but not assumed bias-free.

Two reward models are trained on a CLIP vision encoder: RMM (man-preferred) and RMW (woman-preferred). Table 7 shows strong directional preference: CLIP average PBSG -0.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW -0.7448. steps.notes_before: Section 7/6 concludes that alignment tuning can control gender bias at the action level. Figure 6 shows action-level ΔPBSG changes before vs. after reward-model alignment with RM_M and RM_W. RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals for actions such as exercise, row, and cook, while RMW shifts actions such as bake, sleep, and sweep toward women-preferred portrayals. Figures 6(b,c) rank normalized sensitivity (ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG); sleep, stretch, and read are the most sensitive under both preference directions. The section argues that even seemingly neutral/domestic actions can acquire strong gender bias through alignment and that event-centric evaluation is useful. It also includes a responsible-use caveat: debiasing is not a silver bullet, and representation goals should be set with stakeholder/community input. Earlier tables showed opposite directional reward preferences (Table 7) and opposite effects on the base video model (Table 8: RMM increases PBSG, RMW decreases PBSG).

Section 8 concludes that VideoBiasEval fills blind spots in text-to-video social-bias evaluation by separating identity attributes from content semantics and tracking how alignment changes representation. The conclusion states that reward-based alignment inherits and often amplifies bias in human preference data, so bias auditing and mitigation are needed throughout the video-generation pipeline. It summarizes three evidence points: (1) preference data and reward models show directional biases, with 69.23% (18/26) of qualifying HPDv2 verbs favoring men and 61.11% (11/18) of qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favoring women; Table 4 reports average PBSG 0.6039 for HPSv2.0 and -0.1157 for PickScore. (2) Alignment can amplify inherited bias: Table 5 reports average PBSG 0.8034 for VCM-VC2 and 0.9116 after +HPSv2.0, for Δ +0.1082. (3) Reward design can counter existing bias: Table 8 reports average PBSG 0.8034 for VCM-VC2 and 0.3082 with +RMW.

Section 9 (Limitations) says the study has five main limitations: (1) it uses predefined U.S. Census-style gender and ethnicity categories, which do not capture full fluidity, intersectionality, or cultural nuance; (2) the human-validated VLM evaluators rely on image-level classification and may be biased or inaccurate, especially for stylized/ambiguous frames, though ensembling helps; (3) the experiments mainly test single-step latent consistency distillation with a limited set of reward models, so other alignment protocols could behave differently; (4) the controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations and do not address broader normative or societal-impact questions; and (5) VideoBiasEval is restricted to 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalization to open-ended or novel actions.

Section 10 (Broader Impact) argues that video diffusion alignment can stabilize and entrench bias, making stereotypes appear more natural and authoritative. It also says controllable preference modeling is dual-use: the same method can mitigate or intensify representational harm, enabling correction of underrepresentation but also exclusion, homogenization, or propaganda. The section recommends continuous auditing of social composition with multi-granular event-centric tools like VideoBiasEval and emphasizes rigorous preference-data curation.

Claims/evidence cited here: Table 5 average PBSG rises from 0.8034 (VCM-VC2) to 0.9116 (+HPSv2.0); Table 6 gender rows show mean TAS 0.9763→0.9967 and perfect stability 0.8850→0.9830. Table 7 average reward PBSG is 1.5280 for RMM and -0.7448 for RMW. Table 8 average video PBSG is 0.9584 (+RMM) and 0.3082 (+RMW).

final_notes: Section 8’s limitations: the study evaluates gender and ethnicity using predefined U.S. Census-style categories and notes these cannot capture intersectionality or cultural nuance. It says the VLM-based evaluators are validated against human judgments but may still have biases/inaccuracies in stylized or ambiguous frames. The paper also states the ensemble achieved exact human agreement on every attribute, which motivates its claim that additional annotations would replicate already error-free measurements. The analysis is limited to single-step latent consistency distillation and a limited set of reward models; other tuning methods like RL-based or multi-turn instruction alignment may differ. Controllable preference modeling is only tested via synthetic gender preference manipulations, and VideoBiasEval is benchmarked on a fixed set of 42 socially associated actions, limiting generalization to open-ended or novel actions. Section 7 extends controllable preference modeling to gender. It builds two image-reward datasets from C4Z, each with 2.94 million preference pairs where action and ethnicity are fixed and gender varies (male vs female labels), plus 537,660 R9C face-free pairs for diversity. Two reward models are fine-tuned from pretrained Y2F encoders: Z6B is the Man-Preferred Reward Model (RMM) and P3L is the Woman-Preferred Reward Model (RMW). Table 7 shows Z6B increases average L2V preference scores across all ethnic groups, while P3L lowers them, indicating woman preference. Table 8 shows the same pattern after aligning G4S: +Z6B raises social-bias scores across all demographics, whereas +P3L substantially lowers them and shifts toward woman preference. The text frames this as directional bias control rather than a neutral “fair” reward, and argues that the proportion of man- vs woman-preferred samples can tune a continuous bias/aesthetic trade-off. Figure 6/action sensitivity: Z6B amplifies male-preferred actions like exercise/row/cook; P3L shifts bake/sleep/sweep toward women; sleep, stretch, and read are most sensitive under both directions. The section closes with a responsible-use warning and a call for stakeholder input.

Section 8 concludes that evaluation blind spots require bias auditing and mitigation throughout video generation, not just preference alignment. Limitations: the paper uses U.S. Census-style gender/ethnicity categories, which are socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality; richer intersectional groups are future work. Human-validated VLM judges are still image-level classifiers and can be biased/inaccurate, especially on stylized or ambiguous frames; multi-model ensembling helps but does not remove this. The work mainly uses single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, so RL-based tuning and multi-turn instruction alignment might behave differently. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation shows targeted bias control but does not solve broader value alignment or long-term societal impact. The fixed action taxonomy limits generalization to open-ended or novel actions, so broader culturally grounded evaluation remains needed.

Section 8’s broader impact says alignment can stabilize and entrench bias: improved fidelity/consistency can make stereotypes look natural and authoritative. It warns that curated preference data is dual-use, enabling both bias mitigation and exclusionary/propa-gandistic uses, and argues that aesthetic metrics alone are insufficient. Developers should monitor generated social composition with multi-granular, event-centric audits such as QX2, and curate preference data so it reflects diverse, equitable society.

Section 3.3 adds that demographic attributes are not introduced during generation; analysis happens afterward using three VLM judges (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B). They sample 16 frames per video, then majority-vote frame labels into video labels and fuse across models. Metrics include TAS, PBSG (gender balance), RDS_e, SDI, and deltas for aligned vs. unaligned models. This section defines gender labels as binary (man/woman) while ethnicity has 7 classes.

Section 4 compares two aligned models (InstructVideo, T2V-Turbo-V1) with their unaligned baselines (ModelScope, VideoCrafter-2). Each prompt generates 10 videos; results are averaged. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI) across 42 verbs. Under ethnicity+person prompts, mean PBSG is positive for all ethnic groups; alignment increases PBSG for both pairs (+0.0480 for InstructVideo, +0.0725 for T2V-Turbo-V1). Under person-only prompts, all models overrepresent White individuals; ModelScope has White RDS 0.7690 and SDI 0.0538, InstructVideo has White RDS 0.7833 and SDI 0.0267, VideoCrafter-2 has White RDS 0.6905 and SDI 0.1252, and T2V-Turbo-V1 has White RDS 0.6381 and SDI 0.1119. The table notes that missing values indicate zero recognizable instances for some ethnicities under the person-only condition. Appendix A contains per-verb results, WebVid-10M analysis, and statistical analysis.

Section 4 now includes a human-evaluation validation of the three-VLM ensemble on 400 videos. Three trained annotators checked prompted gender and ethnicity using written guidelines; they made no subjective/normative judgments. The ensemble correlates with human labels at Pearson 0.89 (gender) and 0.73 (ethnicity). Agreement is high: Cohen’s kappa 0.91/0.78 and Fleiss’ kappa 0.92/0.82 for gender/ethnicity. The paper says remaining ethnicity disagreements often reflect frame-level VLM sensitivity to fleeting faces versus human holistic judgment. In a high-agreement subset where human-majority labels exactly match VLM predictions, consensus rates are 99.0% (gender) and 83.3% (ethnicity), and bias metrics stay stable (PBSG 0.846→0.863, p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761). This is presented as evidence the ensemble is a reliable scalable evaluator.

Earlier Section 4 claims remain: aligned models InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 are compared with baselines ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2 over 42 verbs; each prompt yields 10 videos. Table 2 reports ethnicity-aware gender bias (PBSG) and ethnic representation (RDS, SDI). Under ethnicity+person prompts, mean PBSG is positive for all ethnic groups and alignment increases average PBSG by +0.0480 (InstructVideo) and +0.0725 (T2V-Turbo-V1). Section 5 studies social bias in image reward datasets/models. 5.1 analyzes HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic using GPT-4o-mini for caption verb/gender/ethnicity extraction and Qwen/InternVL image classifiers. After filtering, HPDv2 contains 28,783 validated tuples over 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic has 14,958 tuples over 19 verbs. For gender, among verb-specific man–woman pairs, HPDv2 is man-preferred in 18/26 valid verbs (69.23%), while Pick-a-Pic is woman-preferred in 11/18 valid verbs (61.11%). For ethnicity, White is the most preferred overall in both datasets (43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic), with East Asian and Indian next; some verbs differ (e.g., bake→Black, fish→East Asian). The authors argue these preferences may encode Western-centric bias and influence reward training.

Section 5.2 builds a controlled T2I benchmark using FLUX and event templates from Section 3.2. Two settings are defined: Ethnicity+Person (ethnicity explicit, gender omitted) and Ethnicity+Gender (both explicit). They generate 100 images per prompt. Table 3 reports 294 prompts for Ethnicity+Person and 1176 for Ethnicity+Gender, each prompt specifying ethnicity (when applicable), the verb, and context.
